Thus our theologians say that the limit of human life is rightly called both **mobile** and **immobile**. Yet you wittily argue against this: *“Is it not the same limit, however it may be distinguished, since it is a limit?”* At first glance, they indeed seem to engage in a mere war of words <note>original Greek: *λογομαχίαν* (logomachian)</note> and to weary learned ears with empty verbiage, if you consider the limit in itself regarding its very **actuality** <note>original Greek: *ἐνέργειαν* (energeian), a technical term in philosophy referring to the actual existence or operation of a thing as opposed to its potential</note>, as they say. For here that philosophical axiom holds true: *“Everything, while it exists, necessarily exists.”* But because the controversy here is not only about the limit itself—insofar as it already exists in fact, independent of its causes—but primarily about the power and character of those causes; it will be worthwhile to trace back a bit more deeply what they mean by a “mobile limit” and what by an “immobile limit.” By the latter, I believe they designate nothing other than the end of our life in relation to the **First Cause** <note>In Scholastic theology, the "First Cause" is God, whose divine will and decree set all things in motion.</note>—that is, if one considers it within divine foreknowledge...

and disposition, we look at it as a certain future contingency that has been immutably determined. But through the other term <note>Referring to the "mobile limit" mentioned on the previous page.</note>, we consider death as accidental and of an **indefinite nature** <term>ἀόριστον φύσιν</term> <note>original Greek: *aoriston physin*; refers to something that is not strictly defined or bounded by nature</note> in relation to lower causes, which are in their own kind free and contingent. Therefore, although this same limit is certain and in no way to be changed when compared to the immutable decree of the **first and universal cause** <term>τῆς πρώτης καὶ καθολικῆς αἰτίας</term> <note>original Greek: *tēs prōtēs kai katholikēs aitias*; in Scholastic philosophy, this refers to God as the ultimate source of all action</note> and its perpetual concurrence with secondary causes; yet because it is produced freely and contingently by the strength and power of a subordinate and particular cause <note>Such as human choice or natural accidents.</note>, and by its own specific way of operating, it can with very good reason be called changeable and mobile. The leader of the Scholastics <note>Referring to Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Italian theologian and philosopher.</note> declares this to us more clearly when he says:

<margin>Thomas [Aquinas], treatise on Foreknowledge and Predestination, Chapter 4.</margin>

> *The final effect does not follow the first cause in necessity or contingency, but rather the proximate cause; because the power of the first cause is received in the second according to the manner of the receiver, and not according to the manner of that which is received.* <note>original Latin: "Effectus ultimus non sequitur causam primam in necessitate, vel contingentia, sed causam proximam, quia virtus causæ primæ recipitur in secunda secundum modum recipientis, & non secundum modum recepti." This is a fundamental rule of Scholasticism: God (the First Cause) acts through nature and human will (Secondary Causes) in a way that respects the nature of those instruments.</note>

For from where comes the certainty of foreknowledge, if we recognize no decree here? Or does it come from the <term>futurity <note>original Greek: μελλοσίᾳ (*mellosiā*); the state or condition of being about to happen.</note></term> of causes, or of contingent <term>outcomes <note>original Latin: *apotelešmatum*; the results or completed effects produced by a cause.</note></term>? > *You deny that the opinion of even a wise man can be changed; how much more so for God? Since a wise man knows what is best in the present, while to His divinity, all things are present.*

### ON THE END OF LIFE.

...that saying of Epictetus:
> I always prefer what is happening; for I judge what God wills to be better than what I will. *I always prefer what God wills more than what I will. I shall be joined and adhere to Him, as a servant and attendant: with Him I seek, with Him I desire, and simply and in a single word, what God wills, I will.*

Here is the only <term>halcyon peace<note>original: "halcyonia"; a reference to the "halcyon days" of ancient myth—a period of calm amidst winter storms. Van Schurman uses it to describe the mental tranquility found in divine providence.</note></term> for the tides of care; here is the safest harbor for souls wavering through uncertainties; here, finally, is the boundary where I rest both my mind and my pen. Farewell, distinguished man, along with your most excellent wife and dearest children, and specifically with that little daughter whom we have heard you recently initiated into the study of wisdom and languages. <note>Van Schurman was a famous advocate for the education of women; her interest in the correspondent's daughter reflects her lifelong commitment to female scholarship.</note> I pray from the heart to God, the Greatest and Best, that He might deign to bless this most praiseworthy undertaking, and to incite others to imitate you: so that more might learn to compensate for the shortness of this shadowy life with knowledge and virtue.

**Whether the study of Letters is fitting for a Christian woman?** <note>original Latin: "Num Fæminæ Christianæ conveniat studium Litterarum?" We shall attempt to defend the affirmative position.

We set forth these preliminary considerations: first, regarding the <term>Subject<note>In formal logic, the "Subject" refers to the person or thing being discussed—in this case, the Christian woman.</note></term>; and then also regarding the <term>Predicate<note>In formal logic, the "Predicate" refers to the quality or action being proposed for the subject—here, the "study of Letters."</note></term>.

The terms of the Subject are free from all ambiguity; for when I say a **Christian woman**, I mean one who is such both by profession and in reality.

The terms of the Predicate are, first, the **study of Letters**.

# DISSERTATION.

<note>Various passages on this page have been underlined by a reader in brown ink.</note>

By **Study**, I mean (to pass over its other meanings) a diligent and eager application of the mind.

By the term **Letters**, we understand the knowledge of languages and histories, and all the disciplines; both the <term>higher<note>In the 17th-century university system, the "higher faculties" were the professional fields of Theology, Law, and Medicine.</note></term>, which they call the **Faculties**; and the <term>lower<note>The "lower" disciplines refers to the Liberal Arts and Sciences, such as logic, physics, and ethics, which served as the foundation for higher study.</note></term>, which they call the **philosophical sciences**. We exclude only **Scriptural Theology** <note>original Latin: "Theologiam Scripturariam"</note> properly so-called: for we maintain it is beyond controversy that this study is suitable for all Christians.

Secondly, we encounter the word **whether it is fitting** <note>original Latin: "an conveniat"</note>, that is, whether it is expedient, suitable, and proper?

With the words thus distinguished, the things themselves must be distinguished.

For some women are gifted, while others are more dull; again, some are poor, others more wealthy; and finally, some are more, and others less, involved in domestic business or cares.

**The study of letters** is distinguished into either **Universal**, namely when all—

### Limitations of the Predicate.

I define the *Study of Letters* with these limits: I believe that all honorable disciplines, or the universal <term>circle of learning<note>original Greek: ἐγκυκλοπαιδεία (enkyklopaideia). ...we bring forward [arguments] first on the part of the Subject; then also, on the part of the Predicate. <note>In formal logic, a proposition is made of a "Subject" (the person or thing being discussed—here, women) and a "Predicate" (the quality being attributed to them—here, the fitness for study).</note>

### I. *Argument from the nature of the Subject.*

To whomever the principles, or the capacities for principles, of all arts and sciences are naturally granted, for them all arts and sciences are suitable. But the principles, or the capacities for principles, of all arts and sciences are naturally granted to women.

Therefore, all arts and sciences are suitable for women.

*The first premise is proven*: because to whomever the principles or the capacities for principles are suitable, the knowledge of the conclusions—which by their very nature are drawn from those principles—is also suitable.

*The second premise can be proven*, both from the essential form of this Subject—namely, <term>human reason<note>Van Schurman argues that because women possess human reason, they possess the "form" or essence required for learning, just as men do.</note></term>—and from the actual outcomes or effects. Indeed, it is manifest that women do in fact learn various sciences and arts; and no actions can exist without the underlying principles to support them.

<meta>catchword: II. Ar-</meta>

<summary>Van Schurman uses a formal syllogism to argue that since women possess human reason, they inherently possess the capacity for all branches of learning. She asserts that the actual existence of educated women serves as empirical proof of this natural potential.</summary>
<keywords>Logic, Syllogism, Human Reason, Capacity for Learning, Women's Education, Philosophy, Anna Maria van Schurman</keywords>

## II. *Argument from the property of the Subject.*

To whomever there naturally belongs a desire for the sciences and arts, for them the sciences and arts are fitting:

But there naturally belongs to Woman a desire for the sciences and arts. Therefore [they are fitting for her].

*The reason for the first premise is evident*, because <note>original: "Natura nihil facit frustra"</note> **Nature does nothing in vain.** <note>This is a fundamental principle of Aristotelian philosophy: if nature gives a creature a desire or an organ, it must be intended for a specific purpose.</note>

*The second premise is proven*, because that which belongs to the whole species also belongs to each individual. But every human being (as <term>the Philosopher<note>A standard academic reference to Aristotle, who was considered the ultimate authority on logic and science in the 17th century.</note></term> explicitly states in his *Metaphysics, Book 1, Chapter 2*) naturally desires to know.

## III. *Argument from the property or external attribute.*

Whomever God created with an upright face, directed toward the heavens, for them the contemplation and knowledge of sublime and celestial things is fitting.

But God created Woman with an upright face, directed toward the heavens. Therefore [this knowledge is fitting for her].

> *And while other animals look down at the earth,*
> *He gave to man an upright face, etc.* 
<note>Schurman is quoting the Roman poet Ovid from his work *Metamorphoses*. The original Latin is: "Pronaque cum spectent animalia cetera terram, Os homini sublime dedit." In this context, "man" refers to the human species (humankind), including women, distinguished from animals by their physical posture and intellectual potential.</note>

<meta>catchword: IV. Ar-</meta>

<summary>Van Schurman presents two logical arguments: first, that since all humans naturally desire knowledge, women must be included; and second, that the physical human form—standing upright to look at the sky—indicates a divine purpose for intellectual and spiritual contemplation.</summary>

The reasoning for the ***Major premise*** is proved because nothing is more in harmony with human nature than exceptional and honorable pleasure.

# ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN.

### THE THESIS
## OF THE ADVERSARIES.

The study of <term>Letters: the "liberal arts" or academic scholarship, including literature, philosophy, and history</term> is not suitable for a Christian woman (unless she happens to be divinely inspired for it by some peculiar movement or instinct).

#### I. *Argument from the side of the subject.*

To whomever possesses a weaker <term>intellect: original Latin "ingenium," referring to natural talent or mental capacity</term>, the study of Letters is not suitable; And yet, woman has a weaker intellect. Therefore [it is not suitable].

They will prove the *Major premise* <note>The first statement in a logical argument (syllogism) upon which the conclusion rests.</note> by arguing that the study of Letters requires a firm and strong intellect, unless we wish to labor in vain or fall into the danger of <note>original Greek: "ἀῤῥωσίας τῆς διανοίας" (arrhostias tes dianoias)</note> **a sickness of the mind**. They will take the *Minor premise* <note>The second statement in a logical argument which applies the general rule to a specific case (in this case, women).</note> as a self-evident fact.

We respond to the *Major premise*: by our own limitation, those women are excluded who are utterly unfit for studies due to weakness of intellect, since we establish that at least mediocre talents are required here. Secondly, we say that heroic talents are not always—

## II. *Objection.*

To whomsoever the mind does not incline toward studies, for them studies are not suitable:
But the mind of women does not incline toward studies. Therefore [studies are not suitable for them].

They prove the <term>Major premise: the first statement in a logical argument or syllogism</term> because, as the saying goes, nothing should be done <note>original: "invitâ Minervâ"</note> **against the grain** <note>Literally "against the will of Minerva," the Roman goddess of wisdom. This was a common Latin idiom for attempting something for which one has no natural talent or inclination.</note>.

They will prove the <term>Minor premise: the second statement in a logical argument</term> from custom itself; because women very rarely apply their minds to studies.

We respond to the Major premise by saying it should have been stated thus: To whomsoever the mind does not incline toward studies *after all legitimate means have been tried*, for them studies are not suitable. Otherwise, the logical conclusion is denied.

To the Minor premise we say: no one can correctly judge our inclination toward studies before they have encouraged us with the best reasons and means for undertaking such learning, and at the same time offered us some taste of its sweetness. Furthermore, in the meantime, we do not lack examples that prove the contrary to be true <note>Van Schurman likely refers here to historical and contemporary examples of learned women, such as those she corresponded with across Europe.</note>.

*The <term>Major premise</term> <note>The first part of a logical argument</note> is not disputed.*

*They attempt to prove the <term>Minor premise</term> <note>The second part of the argument</note> because* today there are no Academies or Colleges in which women might train themselves.

But we deny this logical consequence: for it is enough that they train themselves at home under the guidance of parents, or some private tutor.

*The Major premise can be proven because the **End** is that for whose sake all things are done.*

## II. Objection.

To whomever the mind is not inclined toward studies, for them studies are not suitable:
But the minds of women are not inclined toward studies. Therefore [studies are not suitable].

They prove the <term>Major premise</term> <note>The first part of a formal logical argument (syllogism)</note> because nothing should be done "against the grain of Minerva" <note>original: "invitâ Minervâ"; a Latin idiom meaning to act against one's natural instincts or without the favor of Minerva, the goddess of wisdom and weaving</note>, as the saying goes.

They will prove the <term>Minor premise</term> <note>The second part of the argument, which applies the general rule to a specific case</note> from custom itself; because women very rarely apply their minds to studies.

We respond to the Major premise that it should have been stated: To whomever the mind is not inclined toward studies *after all means have been legitimately tried*, for them studies are not suitable. Otherwise, the logical consequence is denied.

To the Minor premise we say: no one can correctly judge our <term>Inclination</term> <note>A natural leaning or preference</note> toward studies before they have urged us toward undertaking studies with the best reasons and means, and at the same time given us some taste of their sweetness; though, in the meantime, we do not lack examples that prove the contrary to be true.

<meta>catchword: III. ob-</meta>

<summary>Van Schurman refutes the argument that women are naturally disinclined to study, arguing that a lack of interest is the result of a lack of opportunity and encouragement rather than a lack of innate ability.</summary>

Nor should we think that we are performing our duty excellently if we only look at these things occasionally, as if <note>original: "per transennam," a Latin idiom meaning a cursory glance or looking through a screen or lattice</note> through a lattice. For in that way, we do not see in order to know, but rather we show by this very fact that we do not truly see, because we do not desire to know any further. Nothing is placed before our eyes more wonderful than man; nothing is more beautiful than the <note>The body</note> home of the soul. But how small is that thing which is judged only by the skin, or only by its external appearance? How wretchedly we must blush at those distinguished hymns of the <term>Pagans: "Ethnicorum," referring to classical Greek and Roman philosophers</term>, in which they are accustomed to sing the praises of the <term>Supreme Creator: "summi opificis," literally the "highest craftsman"</term> at every turn while they explore nature more deeply, and through that exploration, come closer to the first cause of all things.

...by a certain **vivid description** <term>hypotyposis: a rhetorical device used to paint a scene so vividly that the audience feels they are witnessing it</term> (as rhetoricians call it), the passion of Christ is represented to us, not only by those words and phrases which place the event as if before our very eyes, but also by external signs and actions of such a kind which, while they renew for us the memory of His wounds and blood and stir up the emotions more vehemently, are accustomed to provide a firm support for our meditation and faith.

On this point, it is not without justice that the saying of that most venerable teacher, *Theodoret*, is cited, where he says that Christ wished for us **"not to focus on the nature of the things seen, but through the exchange of names, to believe in the exchange that has occurred by grace."** <note>original Greek: μὴ τῇ Φύσει τῶν βλεπομένων προσέχειν, ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς τῶν ὀνομάτων ἐναλλαγῆς πιστεύειν τῇ ἐκ τῆς χάριτος γεγενημένῃ ἐναλλαγῇ. Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD) was a Greek-speaking bishop. Schurman uses this quote to argue that calling bread "body" is a "naming" convention of grace, not a description of physical substance.</note>

Whichever way [our opponents] turn here, they are most tightly constrained on all sides; for whether they seek help from the simplicity of antiquity or the subtlety of novelty <note>By "novelty," Schurman likely refers to the Scholastic doctrine of Transubstantiation, which she considers a late and over-complicated invention compared to the "simplicity" of the early Church.</note>, they are forced to acknowledge a **figure of speech**. They cry out that the words of Christ are clear and evident, and therefore do not admit a figure. Now indeed, you have taught them by the most exquisite examples that *it is a common and ordinary way of speaking that what is given for some thing, or is to be in its place, is called by the name of the thing itself in whose place it is handed over.* <note>This is the core of the "symbolic" argument: that Christ called the bread "body" because it was being given "in place of" His body.</note> Furthermore, [our opponents] deny that figurative speech is appropriate for testaments <note>A "testament" here refers to a last will and testament. On the cross, Jesus identifies John as Mary's "son," a clearly symbolic designation of a new relationship, yet part of His final "will."</note> by which, without controversy, He declared His last will. To this truth the Jesuit Salmero <note>Alfonso Salmeron (1515–1585), one of the founding members of the Jesuit Order. "The words of a man's mouth are deep waters" <note>original Hebrew: *Mayim amuqqim dibre pi-ish*; see Proverbs 18:4</note>; or even Genesis 17, where it is said regarding circumcision: *This is my covenant* <note>original Hebrew: *zot beriti*</note>. Regarding the <term>ellipsis: the omission of a word that is understood from context</term> in this phrase, both the 70 Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> and the writers of the New Testament have generally been accustomed to fill the gap with the little word *is* <note>original Greek: ἐστὶ (*esti*)</note>—for it is omitted in the other part of the institution [of the Lord's Supper], namely: *This cup is the new testament in my blood*. 

From this it follows that when Christ said, *This is my body*, it is accurately translated as *this is*, or (which means the same thing) *this signifies my body*. Moreover, even some primary men of high rank from other parties <note>Schurman refers to Roman Catholic theologians here to show that even her opponents' own scholars have doubted the literal interpretation.</note> recommend the opinion that opposes <term>metousia: a Greek term for "change of substance," referring to the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation</term> as being more reasonable and not at all contrary to Holy Scripture.

### ANNA MARIA
### VAN SCHURMAN.

Illustrious man, your most learned letters and the extraordinary gift you have offered me certainly demand an uncommon eagerness to reply; however, a most troublesome cough <note>original: "tussis"</note>, followed by a slight fever <note>original: "febricula"</note>, has prevented me from fulfilling my duty as I ought. And although, due to my health, I have not been able to read through this excellent treatise with precision—a work whose finest parts I rightly attribute to you—I nevertheless do not wish you to be unaware that I have derived no small pleasure and benefit from it. It is incredible how much I am delighted by this kind of subject matter, through which you use the history of antiquity to bring light to eyes that are dimmed by the heavenly radiance. Furthermore, among the other points, your opinion regarding the cross and the hyssop <note>Salmasius was known for his philological and historical research into the physical details of the crucifixion, including the shape of the cross and the specific plant referred to as "hyssop" in the Gospels.</note> greatly pleases me;

For although the copyists <note>The scribes (librarii) responsible for hand-copying manuscripts before the invention of the printing press.</note>, with wavering mind and pen, transcribed them from the **original manuscript** <note>original Greek: αὐτογράφῳ (*autographō*), referring to the lost original documents penned by the Apostles or Prophets themselves.</note>; nevertheless, since we rightly acknowledge the divine providence to be wonderful in the guardianship and protection of this book, there is no reason to doubt its safety. 

And although sometimes certain things may seem **unsolvable** <note>original Greek: ἄλυτα (*alyta*), meaning "insoluble" or "unbreakable" puzzles or contradictions.</note> to us: yet at another time we either easily perceive the truth ourselves, or we find it has been understood by others. For it seemed fit to the **Supreme Deity** to propose to us certain things in His word that appear contradictory, so that even the greatest minds might have a subject in which to exercise themselves throughout every age; and at the same time, He might wipe away all boredom and weariness from them. Not only that, but He also intended to subject human reason to the command of **faith**.

-> # LETTERS <-

...your Letter, in which I certainly approve of those things which you have most learnedly discussed regarding the word **to do** <note>original Greek: ποιεῖν (*poiein*). This verb became a point of intense debate between Protestant and Catholic scholars; Catholics often argued it could mean "to sacrifice" in the context of the Eucharist, while Protestants like Van Schurman argued for a more literal meaning of "to do" or "to make."</note>. Nowhere have I found that word used in that sense—in which that Parisian friend of yours thinks it should be taken—among the Greek writers whom I have happened to see up to this point. I hear that he cites the Greek version of the **Seventy Interpreters** <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, which was widely used and debated in the 17th century.</note>, as is commonly believed by the **Papists** <note>A contemporary term for Roman Catholics, used here in a theological critique.</note>; he contends that they not infrequently used the phrase **to make calves** <note>original Greek: ποιεῖν μοσχάρια (*poiein moscharia*)</note> and similar expressions to mean **to sacrifice**. 

But it is very true that in those places where they provide a literal translation of the Hebrew word **to do** <note>original Hebrew: עשה (*asah*)</note>, they either neglected the spirit and character of the Greek language, or they did not directly and properly designate the act of sacrificing. Furthermore, I do not yet understand how he will prove they ever intended to express the act of **sacrificing** <note>original Greek: τὸ θύειν (*to thyein*)</note> with this word, since this word does not properly and by itself signify "to sacrifice" to the Hebrews, nor have the Greek translators anywhere rendered it with the words **to sacrifice**, **to offer incense**, **to perform a sacrifice**, **to slaughter**, or **to do a ritual** <note>original Greek: θύειν (*thyein*), θυμιᾶν (*thymian*), θυσιάζειν (*thysiazein*), σφάττειν (*sphattein*), ῥέζειν (*rhezein*)</note>, or vice versa translated the Hebrew words **to sacrifice**, **to butcher**, **to slaughter**, or **to bring near/offer** <note>original Hebrew: זבח (*zavach*), טבח (*tavach*), שחט (*shachat*), קרב (*karav*)</note> with the Greek word **to do** <note>original Greek: ποιεῖν (*poiein*)</note>...

# ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN

<meta>The word "fit" at the start of this page completes a phrase from the previous page, likely referring to how a "sacrifice is made."</meta>

...is made. Indeed, it is commonly known that that Hebrew word <note>original Hebrew: עשה (*asah*), meaning "to do" or "to make."</note> accepts a very broad interpretation, so that it signifies not only various and most diverse things depending on the subject matter (if I may speak thus), but also—as you well observe—it sometimes signifies opposites. However, I believe it is written nowhere where it does not equally admit a notion other than that of "sacrificing"; or where it could not be more appropriately explained as "to destroy," "to finish," "to slaughter," "to complete," "to prepare," etc. (examples of which are common in Zephaniah 3:19, Genesis 18:30 and 18:7–8, 1 Samuel 25:18, and elsewhere). 

I pass over for now the fact that neither the Arabic nor the **Chaldean Paraphrasts** <note>The "Chaldean Paraphrasts" refers to the authors of the Targums, which are ancient Aramaic translations and interpretations of the Hebrew Bible.</note> ever rendered the words that properly denote "to sacrifice" using the term **asah** <note>original Hebrew: עשה</note>. However that may be, no comfort is to be expected from this for the **Catholics** <note>original Latin: *Pontificiis*, a common term for those loyal to the Pope.</note>. For if they wish to refer the phrase **do this** <note>original Greek: τοῦτο ποιεῖτε (*touto poieite*) from the words of institution in Luke 22:19.</note> in Luke 22:19 to the body of Christ, the dogma regarding the **unbloody sacrifice** <note>The Catholic doctrine that the Mass is a real sacrifice of Christ, but performed without the shedding of blood, unlike the sacrifices of the Old Testament.</note> will stand in their way; since in the Old Testament, the phrase **to make a calf** <note>original Greek: ποιεῖν μοσχάριον (*poiein moscharion*)</note> and similar expressions are used only regarding animals that are to be slaughtered and immolated, whose blood is poured...

<summary>Van Schurman argues that the Hebrew and Greek verbs for "to do" are too broad to be restricted to a sacrificial meaning, thereby challenging the Catholic biblical defense of the Mass.</summary>

She relies on a comparative analysis of biblical Greek, the Septuagint, and Semitic translations (Syriac and Arabic) to show that such a specific theological meaning cannot be forced onto a general verb.</meta>

...it was seen, they were accustomed to be called: but if indeed they affirm these things are to be referred to the bread, then **to do** <note>original Greek: τὸ ποιεῖν (*to poiein*)</note> will not imply **to sacrifice** <note>original Latin: τὸ *sacrificare*</note>, since nowhere—as you rightly determine—in the **Old Testament** <note>original Latin: *veteri foedere*, literally "Old Covenant."</note> is that kind of offering usually translated [in this way]. This is clearly a flawed progression from a particular instance to a universal rule. 

But because in no place in the **New Testament** <note>original Latin: *Novi Test.*</note> is it found in this sense, nor do the **Arabic** or **Syriac** <note>Syriac is a dialect of Aramaic; Schurman references these ancient translations to understand the "idiom" or language Christ actually spoke.</note> versions (in whose idiom they claim Christ spoke) favor them in any way, we conclude instead that the opposite is true. ...ly, it will be sufficiently clear that these words of the Lord, **"do this"** <note>original Greek: τοῦτο ποιεῖτε (*touto poieite*)</note>, and their purpose—namely, his remembrance—refer collectively (as is very common elsewhere) to the entire ceremony, and especially to the actions of eating and drinking. -> 157 <-

I have no doubt that it [my writing] will nearly bore you to death. I hope, however, that I may easily obtain your pardon if, from now on, I call my mind back to **frugality** <note>In this context, Schurman uses "frugality" to mean brevity or restraint in her writing style.</note>. If that previous discussion of matters did not seem entirely worthless to you, we rightly credit it to you; for you had previously provided us with a most abundant harvest, from which I have gathered this mere **gleaning** <note>original Latin: *spicilegium*. A "gleaning" refers to the scraps left behind after a harvest; Schurman is modestly suggesting her work is just a small collection of ideas gathered from her correspondent’s superior knowledge.</note>. 

Therefore, it would be most fair for you to decide whatever you wish regarding it, were it not for the fact that you view our work with such kind eyes. Furthermore, the subject of that writing was of such a nature that it could easily, as the saying goes, **"stir up the hornets"** <note>A proverbial expression (original Latin: *crabrones irritare*) for provoking a hornet's nest or inciting a heated controversy.</note>. Nor do I think it would serve the dignity of truth if we were to concede anything to our adversaries. 

Certainly, as for our modest **midnight labors** <note>original Latin: *lucubratiunculis*. This term refers to works produced by candlelight or late-night study, often used by scholars to describe their own writings with humble self-deprecation.</note>, if they should achieve even this much honor—that you keep them within the friendly walls of your **study** <note>original Latin: *Musaei*. In the 17th century, a *musaeum* was a scholar's private library or sanctuary dedicated to the Muses, rather than a public museum.</note>...

## To the great city of Dublin, to the honored lady
## Dorothea Moore; <note>Dorothea Moore (c. 1612–1664) was an intellectual and a member of the Hartlib circle, a network of scholars interested in educational and social reform.</note> to the widow of the noble man,
## the freeman Moore; from the city of Utrecht. <note>original: וְטֶרְכֶת (*Utrekhet*). Schurman Hebraizes the Dutch city name Utrecht.</note>

->Peace to my honored lady<-

I have heard of your fame, my friend, honored lady, and I rejoiced and was glad for one of the good things that heaven has bestowed upon us in our days: to renew the glory of your nation. For I had said in the passing of time that wisdom had departed from among the women of England after the death of the Lady Jane Grey <note>Lady Jane Grey (1537–1554) was famously learned in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew.</note> and Queen Elizabeth <note>Queen Elizabeth I (1533–1603) was a noted linguist and scholar.</note> of blessed memory. But peace has come to your heart and knowledge is pleasant to your soul; in you the LORD has chosen to be a crown of glory for all women. A beautiful inheritance has fallen to you, and you have found hidden treasures. Therefore, I have rejoiced in your works as in the rising sun, and I have longed for your friendship. I said in my heart, I will come before your glorious honor with these "ten words" <note>original: עֲשֶׂרֶת הַדְּבָרִים (*aseret ha-devarim*). This is a play on the Hebrew term for the Ten Commandments. Schurman uses it here to modestly describe her short letter.</note> according to my humble knowledge, to strike a covenant of salt <term>covenant of salt: a biblical idiom for an everlasting and unbreakable agreement (Numbers 18:19).</term> between me and you. Let us trade together and acquire wisdom and understanding, for her trade is better than the trade of silver, and her produce better than fine gold. And now, if I have found favor in your eyes, let me know all your desire, and may you be blessed by the LORD. Honor and glory to your nation from the Holy Congregation of Utrecht, in the year of the Messiah [16]41, on the 18th of the month of Av. <note>Av is the eleventh month of the Jewish civil year, occurring in summer.</note>

->Your friend and your servant, Hannah Miriam Schurman<-

Praise is a most pleasant thing to hear, provided that the reputation of those being praised happens to harmonize with the truth. But since, O most praiseworthy of men, the rumor of my devotion to studies has misled you—disposed as you are toward me with a kindness beyond my merit—it would not be right for me to accept the excess of your compliments; for we can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth. <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ δυνάμεθά τι κατὰ τῆς ἀληθείας, ἀλλ’ ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀληθείας" — a quote from the New Testament, 2 Corinthians 13:8.</note> Just as I highly honor all people, both locals and foreigners, who demonstrate wisdom and piety toward God in their lives, so I have no greater ambition than to emulate such people as much as I am able.

# L E T T E R S

...being in a state of envy toward one another; <note>The start of the page continues a comparison, likely between different arts or scholars, which are often prone to jealousy.</note> especially since you seem to have devoted yourself, for the most part, to the art of medicine <note>original: "ἰατρικῇ"</note>. Even if those who have philosophized on ethics <note>original: "οἱ τὴν ἠθικὴν φιλοσοφήσαντες"</note> list it as the greatest of disadvantages of excessive gift-giving—that those who frequently receive a favor <note>original: "χάριν"</note> become more eager to take—you, I suppose, consider it a stroke of luck if you rouse our appetites by promising even more hereafter, into such a desire <note>original: "ἐπιθυμίαν"</note> for future things as great as the pleasure we enjoy when we have laid hold of present ones. I, however, confess that I am never so satisfied with what is gained as not to long insatiably for those things of which you have given us good hopes before now.

# POEMS
## OF ANNA MARIA
### VAN SCHURMAN.

->To the Most Distinguished and Learned Man,<-

## MR. JACOB CATS. <note>Jacob Cats (1577–1660) was a famous Dutch poet, jurist, and Grand Pensionary of Holland. He was a mentor to Schurman and encouraged her literary pursuits.</note>

*Just as they say the resting swan stretches forth its voice,*
*When the breeze of the West Wind has touched its white breast;* <note>original: *Zephyri*. Zephyrus was the Greek god of the west wind, often associated with the arrival of spring and inspiration.</note>
*And as a bird modulates countless songs in its throat,*
*Joyfully marvelling at the new radiance in the sun's orb;*
*So your letter has loosened my sluggish vein* <note>original: *torpentem laxavit... venam*. A classical metaphor for the "vein" of poetic inspiration or talent which had been dormant.</note>
*When your eloquent persuasion breathed upon my heart.* <note>original: *suada diserta*. Schurman likely alludes to Suada (or Suadela), the Roman goddess of persuasion.</note>
*But hence my songs follow the proper laws of meter less strictly,*
*While they rush unhindered, of their own accord, into rhythms.*
*Now I am carried through unknown heavens on Icarian wings,* <note>original: *Icariis... pennis*. A reference to Icarus, who flew too close to the sun with waxen wings. Schurman uses this to express her humility and the fear that her poetic ambition might exceed her ability.</note>
*Having dared to trust in my own strength, which is not secure;*
*Soon the image of fearful Phaethon descends the slopes,* <note>Phaethon attempted to drive the chariot of the sun but lost control. Like the Icarus reference, Schurman uses this to signal her modesty regarding her own intellectual "flight."</note>
*Attempting to go by the headlong path of song.*
*But may my page touch upon your honors, deserved by your virtue,*
*And let it be whatever small part of your praise.*

<header>POEMS OF ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN</header>

Who, though I may sink overwhelmed by the weight of such a massive burden, would not therefore favor my prayers?
Holland, setting aside her other cares along with me, will rejoice to redouble her applause for you;
Just as Cicero <note>original: *Tullius*. Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE) was the Roman Republic's greatest orator and statesman. Schurman compares Cats’ public reception in the Netherlands to Cicero’s fame in the Roman Forum.</note> was received by the public voice when the moved assembly roared throughout the whole Forum.
And why not? Your genius, character, and eloquence urge this, and fortune returns equal marks of favor everywhere.
Therefore, I congratulate our fatherland—or even the world itself—since it wishes to have provided for its own needs more than for yours;
For if such great duties <note>original: *Munera*. This refers to Cats’ "office" or "duties" as Grand Pensionary, the highest political position in Holland. Schurman is noting that his political work takes time away from his "divine songs" (poetry).</note> weigh down your divine songs, what can the pinnacle of honor offer to repair the loss?
If they should destroy so many delights and those sacred inspirations <note>original: *sanctosque furores*. This refers to *furor poeticus*, the classical idea that poets are "possessed" by a divine frenzy or inspiration.</note> with which the hearts of poets are meant to overflow:
Should I not congratulate you on this doubled Duty, since the power of your genius is equal to both tasks?
O, what leisure <note>original: *otia*. In Latin, *otium* is productive leisure or time dedicated to the arts and study, the opposite of *negotium* (business/public affairs).</note> is granted to your happy friends—leisure free from the cares of the State, and not without praise.
Hence, that virginal chorus, more favorable toward studies, joins me in venerating the divinity of the Dutch Muse; <note>original: *Batavæ... Musæ*. The "Batavian Muse" refers to the poetic spirit of the Netherlands.</note>
Hence, any who knows beauty or the grace of pleasant speech thinks it right to speak only in the style of Cats. <note>original: *Catziadæ*. Literally "the sons of Cats" or "those of the House of Cats," referring to his many literary followers and imitators.</note>
My Muse, having come this far as if terrified by her own harsh melodies, leaves these weary sounds in my mouth,
And my final voice scarcely survives the striking of the strings;
O Man, revered by the Fatherland and the Muses, Farewell.

# TO ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN’S PEARL. <note>original: *Unioni*. In Latin, *unio* refers to a large, unique pearl. Her contemporaries frequently used this as a pun on her name and her "singular" status as a learned woman.</note>

->So that she may be less hidden.<-

To what place do you withdraw yourself, O Nymph, for whom all is so well-guarded?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;How long will you lie hidden, buried in silent praise?
The burden of hidden virtue becomes sluggishness, it becomes night;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;rest becomes the heavy image of eternal death.
Come forth, modest Venus, and as a Dutch goddess, 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;be born from the sea <note>A reference to the birth of Venus from the sea foam, reimagined here as Schurman being "born" into public life from a sea of her own intellectual virtues.</note> of so many virtues.
The Sun in the constellation of the Virgin <note>original: *virgine*. An astronomical reference to the sun entering the sign of Virgo, but also a literal reference to Schurman's status as a "Maiden" (*Virgo*).</note> is more than enough; 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;we pray the Virgin be in the Sun; once risen, may you kindle and lead the day.

---

### A RESPONSE TO THE
## HIDDEN ORACLE OF APOLLO
->of a certain person calling me forth into the light<-

The Muse sounds forth a great man; and so that I too might be a poet,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;O Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of poetry and light.</note>, give me your Constant <note>original: *Constans*. A clever pun on the name of Constantijn Huygens (1596–1687), the famous Dutch poet and diplomat who pressured Schurman to publish her writings.</note> genius.
But by what right does he demand that my name become famous,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When the Author, who remains hidden, pleads the case on my behalf?

# EPIGRAM

->ON THE<-
->Most Noble and Excellent Man,<-

## LORD CONSTANTIJN HUYGENS’

### Daily Work. <note>original: *Opus-Diurnum*. This refers to Huygens' major Dutch poem *Dagh-werck*, which provided a detailed account of a typical day in his life with his wife. It was not published until 1638, following her death.</note>

->Which he wrote in honor of his once most-excellent wife,<-
->**Lady SUSANNA van BAERLE.**<-

You ask whether these verses deserve the bright light of day.
Who could deny it? Her noble **GHOST** <note>original: *Umbra* (shade or spirit). Huygens' wife, Susanna, had passed away in 1637; Schurman suggests the publication is a necessary tribute to her memory.</note> demands this for herself.
Even if you wished it, you could not hide your "Daily
Work," for nature itself would resist you, O Apollo. <note>original: *Phœbe*. Apollo was the god of both the Sun and Poetry. Schurman plays on the title: a "Daily" work (associated with the sun) cannot remain hidden in the dark.</note>

---

->TO THE<-
->*Illustrious Man*,<-

## The Lord of ZUYLICHEM. <note>Huygens purchased the manor of Zuilichem in 1630, and was thereafter addressed by this title.</note>

Why do your poems demand me, a mortal, as a witness,
When they have earned the Muses <note>original: *Clarias Deas*. The "Clarian Goddesses," a reference to the Muses who were worshipped alongside Apollo at his temple in Claros.</note> themselves as witnesses?
But your gifts rightly claim my gratitude for themselves;
Since I am unable to repay you in kind, take my name. <note>Schurman modestly suggests that while she cannot match Huygens’ poetic skill, she can offer her "name" (her reputation and endorsement) as a tribute to his talent.</note>

->A. M. van SCHURMAN.<-

### TO AN
# E P I G R A M
->OF THE *Man* השם <note>original: *Ha-Shem*. In Hebrew, this literally means "The Name." While usually a way to refer to God to avoid speaking the Tetragrammaton, here it is used as a pun or a supreme honorific for Huygens as "The Renowned One."</note><-
## CONSTANTIJN HUYGENS
### LORD OF ZUILICHEM,
->which goes as follows.<-

"Have a name," <note>original: *Nomen habe*. In Latin, "having a name" refers to possessing a great reputation or fame.</note> Schurman sings. Most charming
Maiden!
"You have a name" she could not say; she said, "Have one."
Oh, if only she could tell the truth while smiling,
If, by giving what she has, she would grant him to have a name! <note>Huygens is teasingly suggesting that Schurman herself is "the Name" (fame), and that by "giving" herself or her name to him, she would bestow that fame upon him.</note>

---

## RESPONSE
## OF ANNA MARIA
### VAN SCHURMAN.

Since no other is more famous in name than Huygens,
Who could better grant someone a "name" by giving it?

### ANOTHER.

Should Anna believe a name is good when she cannot repay the debt? <note>original: *solvere* (to loosen/to pay). Schurman plays on the idea of a "good name" being like a debt of honor she is too humble to believe she can match.</note>
Who, I ask, can give a good thing which they themselves lack?

### ANOTHER.

Why, CONSTANTIJN, <note>original: *CONSTANS*. Schurman puns on his name, which means "constant" or "steadfast."</note> do you wish to yield your name to ours?
In this way, with the name changed, will you become my "name"? <note>Schurman wittily suggests that if they "exchanged" names or reputations, he would be the source of her fame, rather than the other way around.</note>

## TO THE MOST SERENE
## QUEEN OF ENGLAND
### having recently emerged from childbirth in the year 1635, during the winter season. <note>This refers to Henrietta Maria (1609–1669), the queen consort of King Charles I. In December 1635, she gave birth to Princess Elizabeth.</note>

->E C H O.<- <note>An "Echo poem" is a form where the final syllables of a line are repeated as an "echo" to answer a question or provide a witty commentary.</note>
->Alluding to the insignia of the BRITISH KINGDOM, represented by three roses.<- <note>A reference to the Tudor Rose and the royal heraldry of England.</note>

> What miracles are born for you now in chilly December?
>     Is it because Flora <note>The Roman goddess of flowers and spring.</note>, loathing sterile delays, [produced]? **A Rose.** <note>original: *Rosa*. The echo mimics the sound of the previous word *perosa* (loathing).</note>
> You have conquered the common lot <note>The "common lot" refers to the fact that flowers do not usually bloom in winter; the Queen has "bloomed" by giving birth in December.</note>: and for the English, an everlasting
>     Noble hope of spring smiles. **A Rose.** <note>original: *Rosa*. Echoing *generosa* (noble/well-born).</note>
> Thus may you often be a mother of gods. <note>original: *genitrix Deûm*. In the high-flown classical style of the era, royal children were often compared to young gods.</note> Fate stands and falls
>     While you give birth, or cease, busy Goddess. **A Rose.** <note>original: *Rosa*. Echoing *operosa* (busy/industrious).</note>

## TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS & ANCIENT CITY
## OF UTRECHT
### Anna Maria van Schurman congratulates [the city] on its recently endowed New Academy. <note>Utrecht University was founded in 1636. Schurman was famously invited to write a poem for its inauguration and became its first (though unofficial) female student, attending lectures from behind a curtain.</note>

> You who, powerful by law, rule over the fields, and with high
>     Walls, and lift your massive structures to the stars. <note>original: *moles tollis ad astra*. A classical idiom for grand architecture or high ambitions.</note>

For one whose first care is to shine through talent, and with the arms
    *Of Pallas <note>The goddess Athena/Minerva, representing wisdom and strategic warfare.</note> to drive away dull Barbarism,*
Let the losses of the horn-bearing Rhine <note>original: *cornigeri Rheni*. Roman poets often depicted river gods with horns to symbolize the strength and branching "forks" of a river delta.</note> not move you,
    *Nor that the ungrateful wave has left your household gods.* <note>The *Lares* were the Roman protective spirits of a household. This likely refers to the shifting course of the Rhine or recent flooding in Utrecht.</note>
Let the suspended trade of the greedy crowd not move you,
    *Nor the wandering fortune that once gave fleeting wealth.*
Behold, better waters now flow into the retreating streams,
    *So that your fields may be watered by perpetual springs.*
You see all things joyful shine with a bright countenance,
    *And now your prayers find a place in their own delights:*
For a gracious Pegasus <note>The winged horse of Greek mythology whose hoof-strike created the Hippocrene spring, the source of poetic inspiration.</note> brings new rivers to you,
    *And the charming Muse provides the waters of Castalia.* <note>The Castalian Spring of Delphi was sacred to the Muses; Schurman uses this to metaphorically describe the "waters" of new learning and literature.</note>
From here the native shall drink, and the thirsty *Belgians* <note>original: *Belgæ*. In this period, "Belgians" was often used as a general Latin term for the inhabitants of the Low Countries (the Netherlands).</note> shall drink Nectar,
    *From here one may drink as far as the twin Poles extend.*
From here also, through the eloquent mouths of Minerva’s initiates <note>original: *Mystarum*. Literally "mystics" or "priests" of the goddess of wisdom, referring here to the new university's scholars.</note>
    **YOU, UTRECHT,** <note>original: **TRAIICIES**. A clever pun. *Traiicies* is a form of the verb "to throw across" or "transmit," but it is also the root of *Traiectum*, the Latin name for the city of Utrecht. The poet suggests the city will "transmit" intellectual wealth.</note> will transmit peaceful riches (the gifts of the mind).
But what cares (perhaps you ask) stir your heart?
    *These Sacred rites are not open to choirs of Maidens.* <note>A possible reference to the exclusion of women from the formal university structure, or perhaps the transition from private "virgin" devotion to public civic scholarship.</note>
Here, seeds are sown and harvested by all, so that kind Themis, <note>The Greek goddess of divine law and order.</note>
    *The friend of peace, may keep discordant Chaos from the world;*
And so that Divine Knowledge may shine with pious devotion,
    *And every Altar may glow for the Most High God.*
This is the goal, here I stop; it is enough to have given, amidst the public
    *Joys of the world, these signs of one’s own gladness.*
Hail, O hope of the People, origin of a better race,
    *To whom the Sun of Justice <note>original: *Sol Iustitiæ*. This is a reference to the motto of Utrecht University: *Sol Iustitiae Illustra Nos* ("Sun of Justice, shine upon us").</note> gave the first lights:*
Hail once more, newest Light risen for the astonished ages;
    *May the Sun of Justice never set for you.*

### To the great and noble-hearted
# HEROINE OF GOURNAY,
### Who bravely defends the cause of our sex,
# ANNA MARIA
### VAN SCHURMAN sends congratulations.

You bear the weapons of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of both wisdom and strategic warfare.</note>, a spirited woman-warrior in these battles;
And so that you may win the laurels of victory, you bear the weapons of Pallas.
Thus it is fitting for you to plead the cause of our innocent sex,
And to turn the men's own weapons back against their source <note>original: *in fontes vertere tela viros*. Schurman suggests that Gournay uses the very logic and learning traditionally reserved for men to dismantle their arguments against women.</note>.
Go before us, O glory of Gournay <note>Marie de Gournay (1565–1645) was a prominent French writer and philosopher who argued for the equality of the sexes in her works *The Equality of Men and Women* (1622) and *The Ladies' Grievance* (1626).</note>, we shall follow your standards:
For truly a better cause, stronger than mere force, leads your way.

# ON HER MOTTO
->My love has been crucified.<- <note>original Greek: *ὁ ἐμὸς ἔρως ἐσταύρωται*. This phrase, originally from St. Ignatius of Antioch, was Van Schurman's personal motto. While it traditionally referred to the crucified Christ, she used it to signal that her earthly desires and "worldly love" were dead, replaced by devotion to the divine.</note>

Who would not worship Christ with a restless love?
Whom every knowing Echo <note>In Baroque poetry, an "Echo" poem is a literary game where the final word of a line is repeated or shortened to create a "response" from the character Echo.</note> cries out at the same time: **Love.** <note>original Latin: *Amā*.</note>
He alone loves us, who feeds his lovers with His blood;
He who, by dying, conquered the depths of Hell. **The Rising Sun.** <note>original Latin: *Oriens*. A common title for Christ as the "Dayspring" or "Dawn" in liturgical tradition.</note>
Therefore, wise maiden, seek Him with a chaste mind;
Lean upon this Bridegroom, and do not trust in yourself. **Have faith.** <note>original Latin: *Fide*.</note>

->A. M. van SCHURMAN.<-

It highlights the author’s connection to the wider European "Republic of Letters" and her transition toward deep mysticism.</summary>

# BY ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN

->TO THE<-

## ECHOES OF DOUSA <note>original Greek: ΗΧΟΥΣ. The Dousas (the Van der Does family) were a famous dynasty of Dutch scholars and poets. Schurman is likely responding to Janus Dousa the Younger or his father.</note>

### The Challenge.

->*Whether, having been challenged by the most Noble Man, Lord Dousa,*<-
->*she ought to come forth into the light, or not?*<-

O you Nymphs who echo the songs of the Dousas,
Do not hide what is fitting for me; *Stay hidden.* <note>original: *Late*. This is an "Echo poem," a popular Baroque literary game where the final syllable or word of a line answers a question. Here, the Echo advises her to remain in private life rather than publishing ("coming into the light").</note>

->To the most Illustrious and Distinguished Man,<-

# LORD G. STAACKMANN.

If venerable antiquity teaches us to veil the brow,
And that a maiden’s face should flee the unfamiliar marketplace <note>original: *forum*. Schurman refers to the "public square" of intellectual life, which was often considered inappropriate for women in the 17th century.</note>:
Why is the nature of the soul different for those good things which
Flee the judgment of men, and are sufficient unto themselves?

->A. M. van S C H U R M A N.<-

---

# DEFENSE
## OF ANNA MARIA
### VAN SCHURMAN,

Against certain erroneous rumors, by which—on account of the similarity of the name "Schurman"—she is believed to have translated d’Urfé’s *Astrée* from French into the Dutch language. <note>*L’Astrée* by Honoré d’Urfé was a massively popular French pastoral romance. Because it dealt with themes of romantic love and sensuality, the deeply religious and ascetic Schurman was horrified by the rumor that she had translated such "wanton" material.</note>

Why is there a rumor that my name is woven into such wanton pages?
Why has such a sinister rumor earned belief?

<meta>catchword: An (intended for the next word "Anxius")</meta>

<summary>This page features Schurman’s poetic reflections on her public identity, specifically her hesitation to publish her work and her firm denial of being the translator of a popular romance novel.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Defense" of Anna Maria van Schurman started on page 265. She is clarifying that she is not the translator of the popular French romance *L'Astrée*, which had been mistakenly attributed to her due to a similarity in names. She then pivots to a formal epigram praising Johannes Isacius Pontanus’s historical work on the region of Guelders.</meta>

<header>BY ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN.</header>

*Can the mere trickery of a doubtful rumor have such power,*
*That I should be believed to have abandoned my own character?*
*Not everyone cares for the same things. And such a work* <note>original: *tale meretur opus*. She refers to the Dutch translation of the romance *L'Astrée*.</note>
*Deserves myrtle wreaths—which I have never sought.* <note>The myrtle tree was sacred to Venus, the goddess of love; Schurman implies that romantic literature is beneath her serious scholarly and religious focus.</note>
*I do not envy the lady who wrote it; let her bear the rewards*
*Of her pleasant labor: a different love of art holds me.*
*It helps to have given this warning; lest Venus boast*
*That she has sent the unconquered Muses under her scepter.* <note>The "Muses" here represent Schurman’s intellectual pursuits, which she refuses to surrender to the "scepter" of romantic or worldly fiction.</note>
*Nor shall I be thought to have violated your laws, Astraea:*
*For you yourself command that to each his own should be given.* <note>A clever double-entendre. Astraea was the goddess of Justice (whose motto was "to each their due"), but *Astrée* was also the name of the book Schurman was accused of translating. She is "giving justice" by returning the credit to the rightful author.</note>

# EPIGRAM
->ON THE<-
## HISTORY OF GUELDERS
->By the most Illustrious Man<-
### JOHANNES ISACIUS PONTANI. <note>Johannes Isacius Pontanus (1571–1639) was a celebrated Dutch-Danish historian and the official historiographer of the province of Gelderland (Guelders). His *Historia Gelrica* was published in 1639.</note>

The Sicambri <note>An ancient Germanic tribe who lived in the region of the Rhine and were considered ancestors of the people of Guelders.</note> once cultivated the arts of Pallas Athena,
And their fortune was bright both in the gown of peace and in war,
But now, in an ungrateful age, the glory of that ancient people
Was almost submerged in the waters of Lethe. <note>In Greek mythology, the river Lethe caused those who drank from it to forget their past; Schurman suggests the history of the region was being forgotten.</note>
Devoted Pontanus calls this glory back from the unremembered underworld
And restores such great lights to his fatherland’s soil.
Here he records the sacred counsels, the sayings of great men,
And deeds worthy of the Frankish name:
The rewards which fair antiquity once gave to great spirits,
He makes our age admire.
Thus at once he rightfully claims eternal triumphs for virtue,
And restores ancient trophies to his people.

<meta>catchword: Ann</meta>

<summary>Schurman concludes her poetic defense against being misidentified as a romance translator and provides a commendatory poem for Johannes Isacius Pontanus's history of Guelders.</summary>

# TO THE MEMORY
### Of the most Celebrated Historian and Jurist
## ARNOLDUS BUCHELIUS <note>Arnoldus Buchelius (1565–1641), also known as Aernout van Buchell, was a prominent Dutch humanist, lawyer, and antiquarian. He was a close friend of Schurman's family and a key figure in the intellectual life of Utrecht.</note>
### For his most learned NOTES
### ON
## THE HISTORY OF UTRECHT
### Together with an account of his final days.

> As long as the grace of learned Minerva shall be pleasing to me, <note>Minerva was the Roman goddess of wisdom, medicine, and the arts. Schurman uses her here to represent the pursuit of knowledge.</note>
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Your grace, Buchelius, shall also be sweet.
> For though death takes away the fellowship among men,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nothing prevents you from living on in a mindful heart.

> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So now virtue itself is always the image of you to me.

> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Has deserved never to die, even after his fate is sealed.

<page-num>268</page-num>
<header>ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN</header>

### *On the Reverend, Noble, and most Learned Man,*
## MASTER ANDRÉ RIVET <note>André Rivet (1572–1651) was a prominent French Huguenot theologian and professor at Leiden. He was a significant mentor to Schurman and a frequent correspondent.</note>
### Doctor of Sacred Theology
# V I N D I C A T I O N
->OF MARY, the mother of the Lord.<- <note>This poem praises Rivet’s work *Apologia pro Virgine Maria* (1639), a treatise where he defended the Reformed view of Mary, arguing she should be honored but not worshipped as a divine figure.</note>

*Sacrilegious error had at last pervaded all things,*
*And now powerful Rome was mixing earth with Olympus.* <note>Olympus: In keeping with the humanist style of the era, Schurman uses the classical Greek mountain of the gods to represent Heaven. She is critiquing the Roman Catholic Church for what she perceives as blurring the lines between the divine and the earthly.</note>
*Neither could it be discerned what the true appearance*
*Of the venerable Virgin was: for there was one single face for both*
*The Mother and the Offspring, and a similar worship in all things.* <note>Schurman argues that the Catholic "cult of Mary" made the mother indistinguishable from her son, Jesus, in terms of the worship she received.</note>
*Rivet, burning in spirit, had seen these things, and at once*
*He tears away these masks, and adorns the Virgin’s brow*
*With her own proper colors, sought from the primary source.* <note>original: *primo de fonte*. This is a reference to the "fountain-head" of the Holy Scriptures, which Protestants held as the only pure source of doctrine.</note>
*Indeed, he overthrows the altars of a wrongly fashioned deity,*
*And restores to the world the deserved honors of the great mother*
*(Such as genuine modesty advises).*
*Here, if simplicity depicted on bright tablets should happen to please,*
*The author shall be celebrated throughout the whole world.*

->ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN<-

<summary>Anna Maria van Schurman praises the theologian André Rivet for his work defining a Protestant "Vindication" of the Virgin Mary, which sought to strip away what the Reformers saw as superstitious Catholic excesses and return to a biblical view of her character.</summary>
<keywords>André Rivet, Virgin Mary, Reformation theology, Protestantism vs Catholicism, idolatry, Holy Scripture, religious poetry</keywords>

->To the most Noble and Learned of Heroes,<-
## MASTER CLAUDE SAUMAISE <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), known as Salmasius, was a world-renowned French classical scholar and philologist who held a prestigious position at the University of Leiden. He was considered one of the greatest intellectuals of the 17th century.</note>
->congratulations on his happy return from France<-
# ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN.

Greetings, guest, at last returned to the Batavian lands: <note>original: *Batavis... terris*. "Batavia" was a common humanistic name for the Netherlands.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Indeed, let the world resound: "Greetings, Batavian Guest."
Whom the allurements of Kings, whom so many promises of the Powerful
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Could not even return to your ancestral soil.
From this, Salmasius, what honors shall we not pay to you?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You who preferred us to the honors of your own people.
Now also there is a report that you, bravely for the sake of our altars,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Are laboring on a supreme work of Religion.
Baronius, that worst interpreter of the ancient age, <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607) was a Catholic Cardinal and historian. His *Annales Ecclesiastici* was a massive history of the Church written to defend the Catholic tradition; it became a primary target for Protestant scholars like Salmasius.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Straightway felt the presence of avenging threats.
And although he mimics the massive giants in bulk,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Believe me, he will soon fall by your pen.
Why not? Since the heart of the sevenfold Lerna <note>Lerna: Refers to the Lernean Hydra, the many-headed monster killed by Hercules. Schurman is comparing the Catholic historian Baronius to the Hydra, and Salmasius to Hercules.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Scarcely draws breath, having already been struck by your lightning.
Olympus rightly decrees this contest for you,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So that it may prepare trophies worthy of its own Hercules. <note>original: *Alcidi*. Alcides is a common patronymic for Hercules.</note>
But if you do not disdain the prayers of my sex,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It, too, will freely bring you pleasing rewards.
The charming breath of girls will accompany your triumphs;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And a virgin choir will sing joyful songs.
If this concern seems more fitting to be handled by men,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It is nevertheless not foreign to our forum. <note>Schurman often defended the right of women to participate in the "Republic of Letters" and theological discourse.</note>
Since you strive for a Virgin, while Caesar strives for a She-Wolf, <note>original: *Lupa*. The She-Wolf is a symbol of Rome. Schurman contrasts the Roman Catholic Church (the She-Wolf) with the "Virgin" (symbolizing either the purity of the Reformed Church or the Virgin Mary as discussed on the previous page).</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Why should a virgin not give you laurel wreaths?

->Utrecht, January 3, 1644.<-

<header>ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN.</header>

->To the Reverend, Most Distinguished, and Most Learned Man,<-

# MASTER FRIEDRICH SPANHEIM <note>Friedrich Spanheim the Elder (1600–1649) was a prominent Professor of Theology at Leiden. He was a close friend and intellectual mentor to Schurman.</note>

->Sends many greetings.<-

## ANNA MARIA
### VAN SCHURMAN.

*Why, Spanheim, do you call me back to the streams of Helicon,* <note>Helicon was a mountain in Greece sacred to the Muses; she refers here to the art of writing secular poetry.</note>
*And command me to strike my neglected lyre?* <note>original: *chelyn*. A Greek-derived word for a lyre or tortoise-shell harp.</note>
*Believe me, my songs are not worthy of the sublime cedar,* <note>Ancient Romans used cedar oil to preserve important manuscripts; to say a work is "worthy of cedar" means it is a masterpiece destined for immortality.</note>
*Nor are they worthy of the light of your gaze.*
*Yet it is better to sacrifice to an unwilling Minerva* <note>original: *invitâ... Minervâ*. A Latin proverb for attempting a task without natural talent or divine inspiration.</note>
*Than to deny you the small gifts you desire.*
*With you as my leader, I follow willingly; for your footsteps*
*Will show the way to heaven, like milky signs.* <note>A reference to the *Via Lactea* or Milky Way, used here as a metaphor for a divine or celestial path.</note>
*Often in the past I admired the ancient Greeks,* <note>original: *Pelasgos*. A poetic name for the earliest inhabitants of Greece.</note>
*To whom the first glory of the Muses was given.*
*In my judgment, the world had seen no work more beautiful*
*Than Hesiod, or any greater than great Homer.*
*Already I believed those voices to be pure divine oracles,*
*Which learned Greece celebrates as the Seven Sages.* <note>original: *septem Græcia docta virûm*. The Seven Sages were semi-legendary philosophers and statesmen of the 7th and 6th centuries BCE.</note>
*Now the Academy, with its noble and radiant face,* <note>The Academy was the school founded by Plato in Athens.</note>
*Seemed to touch the starry pole with its summit.*
*Why should I mention the names of Athens, or the great names of the Lyceum?* <note>The Lyceum was the school founded by Aristotle.</note>
*They were like a health-giving star.*
*Indeed, the Stoa, that once-famous cultivator of the unconquered mind,* <note>The Stoic school of philosophy, which emphasized virtue and emotional self-regulation as the path to happiness.</note>
*Had bent my heart to its own devotion.*
*I was then tossed about by this empty care and study,*
*Seeking safe shores in the middle of the sea.*

<sig>A</sig>

<summary>In this poetic letter to the theologian Friedrich Spanheim, Anna Maria van Schurman reflects on her transition from an early obsession with classical Greek literature and Stoic philosophy toward a more focused Christian life.</summary>
<keywords>Anna Maria van Schurman, Friedrich Spanheim, Helicon, Homer, Hesiod, Plato's Academy, Aristotle's Lyceum, Stoicism, classical education, Christian humanism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the poetic epistle to Friedrich Spanheim. Schurman describes her transition from secular, classical learning (symbolized by the goddess Pallas Athena) to divine wisdom (symbolized by the "divine Word"). She explains that while she once admired the Greek philosophers and lawgivers, she now finds their insights insufficient compared to the eternal truths of scripture.</meta>

<page-num>271</page-num>
<header>P O E M S.</header>

*But when the grace of the divine Word deigned*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*To scatter a brighter light into our minds:*
*Just as the stars vanish at the rising of the Sun,* <note>original: *Titanis*. Titan was a common poetic name for the sun god Helios or Apollo.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*So did the torches of dark Pallas perish.* <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom; here she represents human or secular philosophy which seems "dark" or dim compared to divine revelation.</note>
*Truly, human science could not help but lower*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Its majestic symbols of power* <note>original: *fasces*. In ancient Rome, these were bundles of rods and axes symbolizing a magistrate's authority.</note> *before so great a Goddess.* <note>The "Goddess" here is a personification of Divine Wisdom or Theology.</note>
*Then, moistening my heart with nectar-like juice,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Heavenly Persuasion* <note>original: *Suada*, the Roman goddess of eloquence and persuasion.</note> *seemed to speak to me in this way:*
*“What are you doing, O foolish Maiden? Why do you seek with an empty*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Throat the feasts of Tantalus,* <note>In Greek mythology, Tantalus was punished with eternal hunger and thirst, always reaching for food and water that receded from him. Schurman uses this as a metaphor for the unsatisfying nature of worldly knowledge.</note> *which can never satisfy you?*
*Believe me, the tasteless waters that the earth brings forth*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Cannot relieve the burning thirst of the soul.*
*For that which the spirit desires is not mortal like itself;*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*The sacred page alone will provide this.*
*This teaches the mind to embrace the immense Thunderer,* <note>original: *Tonantem*. A classical title for Jupiter, which Schurman frequently uses to refer to the Almighty God.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Whom the very mechanism of the universe cannot contain.*
*Here you will find true rest, and you will be able*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*To safely despise the shifting whims of powerful Fortune.*
*Neither the Samian Mystics* <note>The followers of Pythagoras, who was born on the island of Samos. They were known for their asceticism and their "mystic" silence.</note> *taught such stillness,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Nor did the Actaean Old Man* <note>Socrates, who was from the region of Attica (also called Actaea), where Athens is located.</note> *reveal it with his peaceful voice:*
*The decrees of the lawgiver Lycurgus* <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> *do not mention these sayings,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Nor is the wise and truthful Solon* <note>The famous Athenian statesman and poet, counted among the Seven Sages of Greece.</note> *acquainted with them:*
*Here even the divine insight of Plato fails; and Aristotle,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*That great light of nature, grows dim.*
*Indeed, they instead substituted the perishable gifts*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Of this mortal life for the Highest Good.*
*And since (as they claim) death is the final boundary of all things,* <note>original: *mors ultima linea rerum*. A reference to a line from the Roman poet Horace (*Epistles* 1.16.79), meaning death is the end of the "race" of life.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Death is rightly believed by them to be the ultimate evil.*
*O miserable life! which a brief span of time*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Closes, and black night weighs down with an eternal yoke.”*

<meta>catchword: But</meta>

<summary>In this portion of the poem, Schurman describes her intellectual conversion, arguing that classical Greek philosophy and law—while impressive—cannot satisfy the soul's thirst for eternal truth, which is found only in Christian scripture.</summary>
<keywords>Christian theology vs. classical philosophy, Pallas Athena, Tantalus, Pythagoras, Socrates, Lycurgus, Solon, Plato, Aristotle, divine revelation, mortality</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the poetic epistle to Friedrich Spanheim. In the previous page, Schurman described how the "dark Pallas" (secular philosophy) was eclipsed by the light of the divine Word. This page shifts to a critique of the Stoic philosophers and their view of death and the afterlife.</meta>

<page-num>272</page-num>
<header>BY ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN</header>
<meta>catchword: Hac</meta>

*Or rather call it a fortunate death! whose threads,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Which must not be delayed, Lachesis* <note>One of the three Fates in Greek mythology, specifically the one who measured the thread of life.</note> *finishes with a swift spindle.*
*Behold the high-minded Brutus, and the rigid Catos,* <note>Marcus Junius Brutus and Cato the Younger, famous Roman statesmen who committed suicide to avoid living under a tyrant or losing their political cause.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*How they arm their own hands against their own fates.*
*What madness is it to have wanted to seem like brave and strong men,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Yet not to have endured the unwelcome delays of life?*
*What madness is it to have so often called this light blessed,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*If to live is a punishment, and if there is any safety in perishing?*
*Cease to marvel at the honorable appearance of virtue,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Which has the spirit of a more splendid vice.* <note>Schurman reflects a common theological view that "pagan virtues" were merely "splendid vices" because they were not rooted in faith in God.</note>
*But if the Athenian writings* <note>original: *Cecropiae chartae*. Cecrops was the mythical founder of Athens; Schurman refers here to the works of Greek philosophers like Plato.</note> *could bring back*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*The golden ages to their disciples after death:*
*And if the page had not deceived its friend,* <note>Probably a reference to Cleombrotus of Ambracia, who is said to have jumped to his death after reading Plato's *Phaedo* (a dialogue on the immortality of the soul) to reach the afterlife sooner.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Whom it sent to a headlong death:*
*What would it have displayed except the empty forms of things,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Which it reckoned could make funeral pyres happy?*
*Indeed, in this lay hidden the mercy of the First Cause,* <note>A philosophical term for God as the ultimate origin of all things.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Through whom death is without life, and under whose guidance to die is to live.*
*Let there further be sweet comforts in the Elysian fields,* <note>The final resting place of the heroic and virtuous in Greek mythology.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*And let the Phrygian boy* <note>original: *Phrygius puer*. Refers to Ganymede, the beautiful youth kidnapped by Zeus to serve as the gods' cupbearer.</note> *mix joyful cups;*
*And let there be great pleasure for the souls of Heroes after their fates,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*To fly through the stars and the ethereal homes:*
*And in whatever way the profane Muse plays with the light crowd*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Under an image—suppose she can actually give what she feigns:*
*What would she contemplate but the joys of bodily sense,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Joys such as those found in charming sleep?*
*I pass over the fact that she worships unbridled morals as her own Divinities,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*While she makes shameful Gods with her sacrilegious art.*
*But that Wisdom which has descended from high heaven,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Alone is wiser than all human minds.*

<summary>Anna Maria van Schurman critiques the Stoic ideal of suicide and the "splendid vices" of classical philosophy, arguing that the Greek concepts of the afterlife (like the Elysian Fields) are merely sensory illusions compared to true Divine Wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Stoicism, suicide, Brutus, Cato, Lachesis, Athens, Plato, Elysian Fields, Ganymede, Divine Wisdom, Christian philosophy, paganism</keywords>
