<header>P O E M S.</header>

*Although that one* <note>Referring to secular philosophy or the "dark Pallas" mentioned previously.</note> *may stir up great spirits; yet*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*This other one* <note>Divine Wisdom or Theology.</note> *will bring more to your prayers.*
*She does not only command us to hope for eternal salvation,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*But is able to make everyone blessed before the dark day of death.*
*Why should I recount every detail? Why should I test your ears with my voice?*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Such things are usually felt only by the mind.*
*Then I, praying to her, said: “Grant pardon for my tender years,* <note>Schurman often used the trope of "tender years" or "modest girlhood" to deflect criticism of her learning, despite her great erudition.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*O Goddess, be appeased; it is right for me to follow your commands.”*
*“Do not hasten to withdraw yourself from our eyes,” I pleaded,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*“Nor turn back your step as soon as you have arrived.”*
*She replied to me, however: “My destiny and my origin forbid me*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*From lingering any longer in this worldly region.”*
*“I have not a few Students of rare piety,” she said,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*“To whom I have granted the right to reveal the laws of my court.”*
*“But if you desire to know the sacred things of such a great kingdom,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*And those things which the wave of the Lethean lake* <note>original: *Lethæi... lacus*. In mythology, Lethe was the river of forgetfulness; here it represents the oblivion of death or worldly ignorance.</note> *cannot snatch away;”*
*“And what will not have been learned in vain for the dwelling-place of the blessed,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Then let it delight you to consult these men in times of doubt.”*
*She had spoken, and she left sharp spurs within my heart,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*And set my breast on fire with a sacred love for her.*
*Hence, those whom she had designated as her foremost friends,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*I could not help but honor with the greatest devotion.*
*Among these—just as the Moon among the lesser stars—*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Stands out, **FREDERICK**, your Name.*
*With you leading the way, I shall sing of greater things; and perhaps,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*With you leading, I shall sing songs not unworthy of the heavy buskin.* <note>The "buskin" (*cothurnus*) was the high boot worn by ancient tragic actors; it symbolizes high-style, serious, or epic poetry.</note>
*Just as a rival Echo resounds through the valleys:*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*So I will repeat rhythms that are submissive to your words.*
*Farewell to the Gorgonean springs,* <note>The fountain of Hippocrene on Mount Helicon, which was said to have been struck open by the hoof of the winged horse Pegasus, who was born from the Gorgon Medusa.</note> *and farewell to the learned Sisters;* <note>The nine Muses of classical mythology.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*You shall be my Parnassus, and you shall be my Phoebus.* <note>Phoebus Apollo, the god of light and poetry who resided on Mount Parnassus. Schurman is saying that she now looks to Spanheim for inspiration rather than the pagan gods.</note>

->*Utrecht,* January 22, 1644.<-
<sig>S</sig> <note>Signature for Schurman.</note>

<header>BY ANNA MARIA van SCHURMAN</header>

# ON THE DEATH
## of the Most Noble and Venerable Theologian
# JOHANNES POLYANDRY
## VAN KERCKHOVEN. <note>Johannes Polyander van den Kerckhoven (1568–1646) was a highly influential Dutch Calvinist theologian and a professor at Leiden University. He presided over the Synod of Dort.</note>

Fortunate old man, once while life remained,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;What fortune did not smile as a friend upon your prayers?
Who will boast of more honors worthy of his merits,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which the sacred toga <note>original: *toga sacra*. This refers to the academic and clerical robes of a doctor of theology or a minister.</note> bestowed upon its initiates? <note>original: *Mystas*. A term borrowed from ancient Greek mystery religions, here used poetically to describe ministers of the Gospel.</note>
Who has seen his sons more happily win the court
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of a great Prince for themselves through their duties? <note>Polyander’s son, Jan Polyander van den Kerckhoven (Lord of Heenvliet), was a prominent diplomat and advisor to the Prince of Orange.</note>
Yet one thing was lacking to these, which long old age,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And heavy care upon the earth are wont to deny:
Namely, that while always seeking rest for himself in this world,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;He might be able to enjoy the rest of a peaceful death.
Hence you might also rightly call him blessed after his passing,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If Polyander now possesses everything he sought.
As once the name of Achilles was fortunate and memorable,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;With the Mæonian <note>original: *Mæonide*. An epithet for the poet Homer, who was said to be from Mæonia (Lydia).</note> singing of his deeds:
So are you fortunate, while Spanheim <note>Friedrich Spanheim the Elder, a friend of Schurman, delivered the funeral oration for Polyander in 1646.</note> consecrates
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Your ashes with a learned mouth for a mindful age.

->A. M. van SCHURMAN.<-

# FUNERAL LAMENT
### ON THE
# DEATH
->*Of the Man most Distinguished in Learning and Piety*<-
## MASTER MEINARDUS SCHOTANUS. <note>Meinardus Schotanus (1593–1644) was a professor of theology at the University of Utrecht. He was known for his extreme dedication to his students and his duties, which Schurman suggests led to his early death.</note>

> Who, Schotanus, would not sigh for you, now taken away,
> Nor weep for your passing with a swan-like song? <note>original: *cygnæâ voce*. In classical mythology, the swan sings a beautiful song only once, just before it dies.</note>
> You, who shone from every side with so many divine gifts,
> By which you were born for our sake rather than your own.
> And so that you might be able to grant new life to mortals,
> It did not grieve you to hasten your own death.
> It was not a thirst for silver, nor the worldly business of others,
> Nor the idle lingering at a magnificent banquet;
> But that heavenly ardor which scorched your innermost heart,
> It is what forbade you from counting out a long span of days.
> But although the ethereal fire has consumed you utterly:
> Nevertheless, like the Phoenix, you are born from this very pyre.
> While piety lives, and modesty with a gracious countenance,
> And faith rejoicing in snow-white simplicity;
> While virtue, soothing wild hearts with its persuasive power,
> A glory worthy of your name shall be born.
> Your lot does not require bitter tears, but ours does:
> For your death was a punishment to us, not to you.
> Who could recount the loss of such a great person? <note>original: *tanti capitis*. Literally "of so great a head," a Latin idiom for a person of great importance.</note> It will be
> Better to cover these things with a veil, in the manner of Timanthes. <note>Timanthes was an ancient Greek painter famous for his depiction of the Sacrifice of Iphigenia; he painted a veil over the face of Agamemnon because the father's grief was too intense to be captured by art.</note>
> But it delights me to recall your triumphs in a noble death,
> And the widespread gifts of the high heavens.

*What Divine mother gave birth to your line? Did the learned Carmenta* <note>original: "Carmenta." While "portent" can mean an omen, here Barlaeus uses it to describe Schurman as a "prodigy" or something so extraordinary it seems to defy the natural order of the time.</note>

# TO ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN.

*Shall I say that Jove has erred? Or that male likenesses are being transformed in wondrous ways? A second Sempronia* <note>original: "Sempronia." A Roman woman praised by Sallust for her knowledge of Greek and Latin literature, though criticized for her character; Barlaeus uses her here as a symbol of female erudition.</note> *is born to us, and a Sappho* <note>original: "Sappho." Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom, who was born from the head of Zeus (Jupiter).</note> *to the lands, and a woman examines ancient Athens.* <note>Athens here represents the study of the Greek language and philosophy.</note>
*Neither Latium nor Rome is enough; it is not sufficient for her to speak with a single tongue; simple eloquence is less than the desires of this Virgin. Anna reads even the Argolic* <note>original: "Argolicas." A poetic term for Greek.</note> *voices (o gods!), and unites her Belgian heritage with Cecrops.* <note>original: "Cecrope." Cecrops was the mythical founder and first king of Athens; Barlaeus is saying she unites Dutch and Greek culture.</note>
*If it was a wonder that the writings of ancient Corinna* <note>original: "Corinnae." A Greek lyric poetess said to have defeated Pindar in competition.</note> *were preserved, she too has what she might write. If Manto,* <note>original: "Manto." A prophetess and daughter of Tiresias.</note> *privy to the secrets of things, brought forth her songs in ages past, and the great Sibyls* <note>original: "Sibyllae." Prophetesses of the ancient world whose oracles were highly prized.</note> *sang something extraordinary, this mind of Maria is capable of the same. Polla* <note>original: "Polla." Polla Argentaria, the wife of the poet Lucan, who was said to have assisted him in correcting and completing his epic poem, the *Pharsalia*.</note> *was joined to a husband and assisted in the commentaries of her poet; nor would she be less able to assist the studies of men, if admitted to the shared marriage-bed. Why do you boast, Belgium,* <note>original: "Belgica." Referring generally to the Low Countries/The Netherlands.</note> *of your warships, and of the wealth of a growing empire supported by a great Prince? Why of your battles spread by fame, your ships laden with foreign goods, and so many cities opened up everywhere with new walls?*
*Marvel at greater things here. She alone completes the rare name of Batavia* <note>original: "Bataviae." The poetic name for the Netherlands.</note> *for you. This eloquent virago* <term>virago: In the 17th century, this was a term of high praise for a woman of extraordinary, "heroic" spirit or masculine strength of mind.</term> *surpasses so many titles, and goes before trivial pride with her virtues. Gender no longer carries a price. O learned men, you share a common mind with this virgin. Only the most worthless portion of us remains our own. Alas, we are distinguished by bodies alone; she mingles her genius and arts with men, and in that part where we are wise, she deserves to be called a man.* <note>In the gender hierarchy of the time, the highest compliment a scholar could pay a woman was that her intellect had "transcended" her sex to become equal to a man's.</note>

*What shall I say worthy of you, Virgin? You who are to be revered for your modesty...*

### BY ANNA MARIA van SCHURMAN.

*And the soldier would desire to fight less, were it not that the fierce and untamable Spaniard* <note>original: "Iber." Referring to the Spanish forces during the Eighty Years' War.</note> *harassed our temples and our hearths.*
*Already the miter* <note>original: "mitra." A symbol here for the faculty of Theology or high ecclesiastical learning.</note> *has begun to speak. The youth, eager for praise, rush forward, and the strong young men burn with ambition.*
*The gods descend to the earth—Piety and Justice* <note>original: "Themis." The Greek goddess of divine law and order.</note>—*and the sacred pulpits resonate with the voice of the mighty God.*
*Nor does Medicine cease to speak. Hearts are shaped by the arts, and all things bear the likeness of one who knows everything.*
*Nature made us unrefined; cultivation and labor polish us, and through this secondary care, the human being is truly made.*
*The wise person must be born twice, and twice given to the world; one is not truly wise until one has succeeded in birthing oneself.*
*That we Dutch* <note>original: "Batavi." Referring to the people of the Netherlands through their ancient tribal name.</note> *still stand, we owe to Apollo* <note>original: "Phœbo." The god of wisdom, light, and the arts.</note> *and to our arms; a suppliant Belgium* <note>original: "Belgica." A common Neo-Latin term for the Low Countries.</note> *prays for this twofold aid.*
*The Prince of Orange* <note>original: "Auriacus." Referring to the House of Orange-Nassau, the military and political leaders of the Dutch Republic.</note> *has that which he must protect, and so does Apollo. The latter defends our minds, the former our homes.*
*O citizen of Utrecht* <note>original: "Trajectine." From Trajectum, the Latin name for Utrecht.</note>, *Anna joins in your new undertakings; the noble Anna favors them with her own auspicious presence.*
*Now the Virgin returns; miracles return to the world. The maiden sees her poets following behind her.*
*We men are surpassed. Let this maiden be what we once were; she seizes for herself the very titles of the poets.*
*O Jupiter, grant this maiden a better sex* <note>A common, if dated, Renaissance compliment suggesting that Schurman's intellect was so great it transcended the perceived limitations of her gender.</note>—*or rather, while everyone stands amazed, declare her to be a Goddess.*
*Call her Pallas* <note>original: "Pallada." Athena/Minerva, the goddess of wisdom and war.</note>—*not the one who brandishes a trembling spear, but the one who, with her voice, stirs the foundations of this rising School* <note>original: "Scholam." This likely refers to the inauguration of the University of Utrecht, where Schurman famously wrote a poem and was allowed to attend lectures behind a curtain.</note>.

# CLAUDIUS SALMASIUS
### *In the Preface to Miscellaneous Definitions* <note>original: "In Præfat. ad Miſc. Defin." Referring to a work by Salmasius.</note>

We have in a city located a single day's journey from here, a noble maiden, who is no less multi-talented in numerous arts than Hippias <note>original: "Hippiam." Referring to Hippias of Elis, a Greek philosopher known for claiming mastery over all knowledge and crafts.</note>, and she is all the more to be admired on that account, because such fertility of genius and such an abundance of skills so rarely befall this sex; since she is skilled in all of them, she is a conjunction of so many virtues that she lacks none. Whatever can be made by the hand or conceived by the mind, she alone masters. She paints so well that no one does it better. She sculptures and molds from bronze, from wax, and from wood likewise. In the art of embroidery <note>original: "phrygionica arte." Phrygian work was a classical term for fine needlework or gold-thread embroidery.</note> and in all things that are the concern and work of women, she challenges and surpasses all women, both ancient and modern.

Indeed, she is equipped with so many gifts of learning that you would not know in which one she most excels. She is adorned with the gifts of so many languages that, not content with European ones, she has flown by study and diligence even unto the East, to acquire there Hebrew, Arabic, and Syriac <note>original: "Syriacas." A dialect of Aramaic used in early Christian texts.</note>, to join them to those she already possesses. She writes in Latin so well that no man among those who have striven for this elegance their whole lives writes more polished prose. She composes such French letters that Balzac <note>original: "Balzacius." Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac, a contemporary writer famous for his elegant French prose.</note> could hardly write better. She uses the other languages of Europe just as well as those for whom they are native. She is able to conduct a correspondence in Hebrew with the Jews, and in Arabic with the Saracens <note>original: "Saracenis." A historical term for Arabic-speaking peoples or Muslims.</note>. She handles sciences that are arduous and thorny even for men—namely, Scholastic Philosophy and Theology—in such a way that everyone is amazed, for the matter is like a miracle; no one may rival her, because no one can imitate her; and no one may even envy her, because she herself is above envy.

# ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN

*And he [the Prince] would desire to fight less, were it not that the fierce and indomitable Spaniard* <note>original: "Iber." A reference to the Spanish forces during the Eighty Years' War.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*harassed the temples and the hearths.*
*Now the mitre* <note>the Church or clergy</note> *has begun to speak; the youth, eager for praise, rush forth,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*and the strong young men burn with ambition.*
*The Gods above descend to the lands—both Piety and Justice* <note>original: "Themis," the Greek goddess of divine law.</note>—
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*and the sacred pulpits sound with the mighty God.*
*Nor does Medicine cease to speak. Hearts are shaped in the arts*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*and bear the image of one who knows all.*
*Nature made us unrefined; cultivation and labor*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*polish us; this second care makes the human.*
*The Wise person must be born twice, and twice returned to the world;*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*nor is one wise unless they were able to have begotten themselves.*
*That we Dutchmen* <note>original: "Batavi." A classical name for the people of the Netherlands.</note> *still stand, we owe to Apollo* <note>god of the arts and intellect</note> *and to arms;*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*the Belgian* <note>original: "Belgica." Referring here to the Dutch Republic.</note> *suppliant asks for this twin help.*
*Orange* <note>The House of Orange, specifically Prince Frederick Henry.</note> *has what he may protect; Apollo has what he may protect.*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*The latter claims our minds, the former our homes.*
*O citizen of Utrecht* <note>original: "Trajectine." Referring to the city of Utrecht.</note>, *Anna joins in your undertakings;*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*noble Anna nods in agreement with her own omen.*
*Now the Maiden also returns; miracles return to the lands.*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*The girl sees her own poets follow behind her.*
*We cease to be men; let a maiden be what we once*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*were. The maiden snatches the titles of the poets.*
*Jupiter, gift this girl with a better sex;*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*or say, while everyone is astonished, that she is a Goddess.*
*Call her Pallas* <note>Athena/Minerva, goddess of wisdom.</note>—*not the one who shakes a trembling spear,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*but the one who shakes the nascent School* <note>original: "Scholam." Referring to the newly founded University of Utrecht.</note> *with her voice.*

<summary>This page contains a Latin poem (likely by Caspar Barlaeus) celebrating the dual defense of the Netherlands through military strength (Orange) and intellectual cultivation (Apollo). It concludes with a panegyric for Anna Maria van Schurman, framing her as a modern Pallas Athena who oversees the new University of Utrecht.</summary>

<header>TESTIMONIALS.</header>

# CLAUDIUS SALMASIUS
## *In the Preface to Miscellaneous Definitions*

We have, in a city situated a day’s journey from here, a noble maiden who is no less multi-skilled in numerous arts than Hippias <note>Hippias of Elis was an ancient Greek philosopher famous for mastering every craft and science of his time.</note>, and she is all the more worthy of wonder because such fertility of genius and such a wealth of arts rarely fall to her sex; for she is skilled in all of them, and possesses a conjunction of so many virtues that she lacks none. Whatever can be fashioned by the hand or conceived by the mind, she alone masters. She paints in such a way that no one does it better. She sculpts and molds from bronze, wax, and wood with equal skill. In the art of embroidery <term>phrygionica arte: literally "Phrygian art," a classical term for the intricate, gold-threaded needlework for which the Phrygians were famous.</term> and in all things that belong to the cares and works of women, she challenges and surpasses all women of both ancient and modern times. Indeed, she is equipped with so many gifts of learning that you would not know in which she most excels. She is adorned with so many gifts of languages that, not content with European ones, she has flown by her study and industry all the way to the East to acquire Hebrew, Arabic, and Syriac to add to those she has already mastered. She writes in Latin so elegantly that none of the men who have spent their whole lives striving for such refinement can write more polished prose. She composes such French letters that Balzac <note>Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac (1597–1654), a famous French author credited with reforming French prose.</note> could hardly do better. She uses the other languages of Europe as well as those for whom they are the native tongue. She is able to carry on a correspondence in Hebrew with Jews and in Arabic with Saracens <note>original: "Saracenis." A common early modern term for Arabic-speaking Muslims.</note>. She handles even the difficult and thorny sciences—namely Scholastic Philosophy and Theology—in such a way that everyone is stunned, because the matter is like a miracle. No one can rival her, because no one can imitate her; and no one can envy her, because she is beyond envy itself.

<page-num>326</page-num>
<header>TO ANNA MARIA van SCHURMAN</header>

## CONSTANTIJN HUYGENS
### From his *Epigrams*.

Your face is pleasing; but why, O Tenth of the Goddesses <note>original: "bis quinta Dearum." A common honorific for van Schurman, styling her as the "Tenth Muse" alongside the traditional nine of Greek mythology.</note>, do you hide your most wonderful part away from that more illustrious side?

That hand of yours, ever restless and new, which never ceases to surpass itself, could not depict itself as uncertain. 
Yet I am not hidden in that part, if you begin to be my reader at the point where you cease to be my spectator. 
With both mind and hand I have rendered my face; but the written word has painted more. The written letter reflects the mind, while the painted one reflects the hand.

### ON THE SAME WOMAN.

Until now, there was only one; but a second Phoenix <note>The Phoenix was a mythical bird that was unique in the world; here, Huygens suggests van Schurman's genius is so singular that she is a second Phoenix, perhaps "stolen" from nature by her own art.</note> is produced by a kind of theft; a private crime results in a public blessing. 
How well she keeps from betraying herself—she who, by fleeing, confesses that her own right hand has stolen a Phoenix from herself!

### ON THE SAME WOMAN.

Anna, I will confess it: you could have been more pleasing when painted, and the beauty of un-carved bronze was no more delightful. 
But you please more when carved. They say a girl is for sale whose cheek shines with much painted color <note>Huygens contrasts van Schurman’s intellectual and artistic depth with women who use cosmetics to attract suitors.</note>. 
She, who loves only virtue and ignores any Lover, is pleased (if it be lawful) not to have pleased by outward appearance alone. 
She who—not harsh toward a few men—if she were to marry, would marry only geniuses with her own singular genius. 
She, being all mind, wishes to be seen by the mind alone; she considers her limbs to be like a weight of superfluous burden. 
Should she shine with hair-remover <term>psilothro: an ancient depilatory cream used for vanity.</term>, or wear white makeup <term>cretam: literally "chalk," used in the 17th century to whiten the skin.</term>? No; she ought to have been carved, and carved by her own hand <note>original: "ungue suo," literally "by her own nail." This refers to her skill as a sculptor and engraver, suggesting her character is best represented by the sharp, precise tools of her own art rather than soft paints or cosmetics.</note>.

<header>TRIBUTES.</header>

## BY DANIEL HEINSIUS
->An extemporaneous poem,<-
->O N<-
# THE PORTRAIT
->OF ANNA MARIA van SCHURMAN,<-
->captured from life by the most celebrated painter JAN LIEVENS.<-

The work of a divine painter, a heavenly image,
->Which this hand, worthy of painting Goddesses, has given,<-
Who, while he wished to paint all the Muses but could not,
->Portrayed the Tenth, and within that Tenth, the other nine.<-
<note>The "Tenth Muse" was a standard honorific for Van Schurman. Heinsius argues that Jan Lievens’ portrait of her is so perfect that by painting her, he effectively captured the essence of all nine traditional Greek Muses.</note>

## GEORGIUS STAACKMANS.

**MOST NOBLE LADY,**

If Utrecht has not cast me further away from you than the cares of The Hague have made me neglectful of you, then all is well. Indeed, let this paper structure blush under such a condition, bearing a <term>rhapsody</term> <note>original: "Ῥαψῳδίαν"; here meaning a miscellaneous or improvised collection of writings</note> instead of a <term>panegyric</term> <note>original: "Πανηγυρισικοῦ"; a formal speech or text delivered in high praise of someone</note>. At the very least, it will show that I still regard you with the same veneration with which I followed your work at Franeker <note>A university city in the Netherlands where Van Schurman had significant intellectual ties.</note>. O happy times! compared to these days in which it is scarcely permitted to perform whatever small duty this is—

### Concerning the Minerva of her age,
# ANNA MARIA van SCHURMAN
### Residing in Utrecht.
<note>Minerva was the Roman goddess of wisdom, weaving, and the arts. Comparing a woman to Minerva was the highest possible compliment for a female scholar in the 17th century.</note>

*Whether I stand senseless in awe, losing the use of my tongue,*
*Or whether I am forbidden to speak by a quiet, sacred dread;*
*Whether it is my sight that fails me, or that which I labor to behold*
*Refuses to be seen because of its constant lightning-flash—*
*Anna, I have known your gifts, yet I cannot describe them.*
*To whom can even the smallest of your merits be told, O Anna?*
*Unless fear and care and silences are pleasing to the Gods,*
*Unless a blind love recommends hearts that are pious:*
*Anna, I shall be ordered by law to remain outside your sacred rites,*
*And I will have scarcely set foot within, as the law commands.*
*To turn over something divine in the mind is a thing full of peril;*
*To bring forth something divine with the voice is more perilous still.*
<note>The poet uses the language of "sacred mysteries" to describe Van Schurman's intellect, suggesting she is so brilliant that approaching her is like entering a forbidden temple where common speech fails.</note>

In this vastness there is a prison; in this light there is darkness, 
  As if a violent night were to cloud the midday sun. 
While I wander through these immense spaces, chains restrain me: 
  While so many things reveal themselves to me, I see nothing. 
Lest I, out of my mind, should enter an unsafe sea with such high thoughts; 
  My ship stands fixed in the harbor. 
Nor should I defile your bright radiance with my impure soot <note>original: "fuligine"; the poet uses "soot" or "smoke" as a metaphor for his own unworthy writing clouding her brilliance.</note>; 
  It is better to place reins upon my pen, and reins upon my hand. 
But a stimulus pricks me again, and is the author of my will: 
  It is a sin to know your gifts and yet remain silent. 
If the Egyptian people <note>original: "Memphitica plebes"; referring to Memphis, the ancient capital of Egypt.</note> had known a similar marvel, 
  Their prodigious stones <note>The Pyramids.</note> would have threatened the very heavens. 
Vain Greece would have dared anything, if only such glory 
  And such true honor had remained untouched for her. 
What temples and sacred couches <note>term: "pulvinaria" (sacred cushioned seats used in Roman rituals to display the statues of gods).</note> would proud Rome not show 
  To her guests, if she possessed such a Goddess? 
Let her divinity still lie hidden, if she protects the Roman citizens; 
  They would wish for nothing else, and would seek her favor. 
Where vile refuse, where a shameful brothel once found worship, 
  And where the shameful form of a dog <note>Anubis, the jackal-headed Egyptian god, often mocked by Roman-influenced Christian writers.</note> was revered: 
Where monsters filled the city during solemn feasts, 
  Maddened, and where their sacred rites professed a rabid sin: 
How many shrines would have been devoted to you, how many altars, 
  **ANNA**, you who hide a Goddess behind a mortal face? 
Let a new Athens arise, greater than or equal to the ancient one: 
  For you are present as a divinity competing with the old gods. 
You are one among the nine Muses, one among the many Sibyls <note>Prophetic women of the ancient world.</note>. 
  Indeed, you are better: should Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom.</note> alone stand before you? 
Legend says she was born from the brain of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note>; but it is your role 
  To have both given birth to and polished true Jupiters <note>The poet suggests that while Minerva was merely a product of Jove's mind, Schurman's intellect is so great that she "creates" and refines other great minds through her influence.</note>.

<page-num>330</page-num>

<header>TO ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN</header>

<meta>catchword: Belgica (referring to the Netherlands)</meta>

From her birth, ruddy gold flowed from heaven:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A golden age adorns your birth.
In her, she granted a triumph over virginity to none:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You too would be far too unyielding for Tiresias <note>Tiresias was the blind prophet of Thebes who, according to myth, had lived as both a man and a woman; the poet suggests Schurman’s purity or intellectual stature is so formidable it would daunt even the most experienced judge of human nature.</note>.
Whatever beautiful thing came from that cruder age;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You make more beautiful by your intellect and your hand.
Do not look back to Orpheus, Praxiteles, or Apelles <note>Orpheus was the legendary musician; Praxiteles and Apelles were the most famous sculptor and painter of ancient Greece, respectively. The poet argues Schurman surpasses them all.</note>; since you
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Are able to count Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom, weaving, and the arts.</note> among your pupils.
Let her be famous as a victor with her Aegis <note>term: "Aegis" (the protective shield or breastplate of Athena, often featuring the head of the Gorgon Medusa).</note>, and the slain Gorgon:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Let Troy <note>original: "Pergama"; the citadel of Troy.</note> have been protected for long by the Palladium <note>term: "Palladium" (a sacred wooden statue of Athena; as long as it remained in Troy, the city could not fall).</note>:
You, whatever walls you enter, protect them even while unarmed;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You have nothing to do with Mars <note>The god of war.</note>; let him rage outside.
Could he whom the naked poet <note>Likely referring to Orpheus, who could charm all things with his music.</note> was able to keep from the threshold,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Endure being a burden to your home?
But indeed, no herds shed blood for you;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;No groves flourish; no bird is consecrated <note>The poet notes that unlike the ancient gods, Schurman requires no animal sacrifice or pagan rituals; her "worship" is purely intellectual and spiritual.</note>.
You surpass and disdain worldly honors;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And in your piety, you deny yourself even heavenly ones.
Let fame give titles to those lacking solid praise; let it decorate
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The unseemly; and let it love those by whom the World is loved:
Honor of the world, and the Pallas of your age, SCHURMAN;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That which others strive for, for you it is enough to have simply deserved it.
We too condemn whatever insane antiquity
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Held as a fabricated likeness of an extraordinary deity:
Whether because of something given to ascend to heaven;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Or whoever traces their lineage from there.
Yet the hearts of the Dutch <note>original: "Belgis"; at this time, "Belgica" often referred to the Low Countries or the Netherlands as a whole.</note> are not entirely blunt;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Such that they would despise what strikes the ears and eyes.
Having cast aside the trappings and pomp meant for the masses;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;They have dedicated themselves entirely to you with inner zeal.

It highlights her role as a source of national pride for the Dutch people.</summary>

<page-num>331</page-num>

<header>ELOGIES.</header>

Even if the laws of the Netherlands <note>original: "Belgica"; referring to the Low Countries/Netherlands.</note> do not proclaim you a goddess;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The nobles, Anna, honor you with the reverence you deserve.
Though no pyramids or monuments rise in your honor:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And the earth bears no statues or carved likenesses of you:
Should you test our Dutch hearts with any command;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nowhere would you find people more willing to obey.
Especially here, where the weary Father Rhine <note>The personification of the Rhine River.</note> once hid himself;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And slowly flowed into unknown waters <note>This refers to the Rhine delta in the Netherlands, where the river meets the sea.</note>.
Where a living piety first shone out: and where
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A failing faith found its own Atlas <note>Atlas was the Titan of myth who held up the heavens; the poet suggests Schurman is the pillar holding up the faith in her country.</note>.
Let the famous city <note>Utrecht, where Schurman lived.</note> take pride in its dual leader <note>term: "Præsule" (a high-ranking leader or prelate, referring here to both religious and civil authority).</note>: for one
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Imbued a wild people with holy customs;
The other acted as king on behalf of the great Emperor; while the Spaniard <note>original: "Iber"; referring to the Spanish Empire, the enemy of the Dutch during the Eighty Years' War.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Gnashes his teeth and trembles at the Dutchman set over him.
What is a leader, unless you—our High Priestess—are greater;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And who is not lesser than you, if he does not rule his own kingdom?
O queen of the shining choir <note>Likely referring to the Muses or the circle of learned scholars.</note>! Even when Juno <note>Queen of the Roman gods.</note> is set aside,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And flees with her torches, you remain.
Let the city walls <note>original: "pomoeria"</note> of Saint Anthony bear your likeness:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For the walls of Franeker <note>The site of the University of Franeker, where Schurman was famously the first woman to attend university lectures.</note> shine continually with your rays.
Even Cynthius <note>A title for Apollo, the sun god.</note> himself, and the moon—the sun's substitute lamp—
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Are accustomed to endure the night, the clouds, and the eclipse.
At such times, no matter how much the eyes strain, shadows
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Play tricks on the vision; and suddenly, where they flickered, they vanish.
But you, a powerful star, flash with a cloudless light:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You alone are the North Star <note>original: "cynosura"; the constellation Ursa Minor, used by sailors as a fixed point for navigation.</note> who guides our wandering eyes.
You alone, with a splendor that never sets, refresh those souls
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Besieged by darkness, and teach them how to overcome.
If the ancient fortress of the Wilts <note>original: "VViltorum castra"; an old name for the city of Utrecht, derived from its legendary early inhabitants.</note> no longer holds you:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Believe that our very hearths <note>original: "lares"; the Roman household gods, used here to mean "homes."</note> depend upon your merit.

# TO ANNA MARIA van SCHURMAN

<meta>catchword: Quanta</meta>

*These people look up to you and, if you allow it, they adore you:*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*They will never be able to forget you.*
*Perhaps those cities applauded themselves more in the past,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*When they threw forty thousand men against the enemy;*
*When neither religion nor* **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sapientia"</note> *held a faithful place*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*In the armed citadel of* **Peace**.
*For shame! Should not a divine heroine* <note>original: "virago"; in this period, the term was a high compliment for a woman of "masculine" intellectual strength and courage.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Surpass several thousands of men snatched from the dregs of the common people?*
**Denmark** *sent her common troops to the underworld;*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*And* **France** *broke the work she herself had built.*
*At last we see roofs raised under new beginnings,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Rivaling the heights of* **Rome** <note>original: "Ausoniis," referring to the Ausonians, an ancient people of Italy.</note>:
*We see a theater* <note>likely referring to the newly founded University of Utrecht (1636).</note> *opened for* **Apollo** <note>original: "Phæbo"</note> *and the* **Muses**:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*You, O* **Athena** <note>original: "Pallas"</note>, *were the sole witness to such greatness;*
*Whether you wish to be held as a resident or more as a citizen:*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Utrecht** *has nothing greater than its* **Athena**.
*Indeed, that school is celebrated in your honor,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*And the learned stages echo with your name.*
*Where else should the interpreter of heaven go; and together*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*With the nourishing* **Justice** <note>original: "Themis," the goddess of divine law.</note> *who draws a great retinue?*
*Where rather should the* **Delian** <note>Another name for Apollo, the god of light and truth.</note> *vibrate his venerable fire?*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Where should the* **group of nine** <note>The nine Muses of inspiration.</note> *bring out their treasures?*
*If I must compete here, let me compete with you presiding:*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*And let me expect worthy rewards from your hand.*
*You, O astounding Maiden, understand whatever* **Phoenicia** *produced,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Greece** *nourished, and* **Italy** <note>original: "Hesperia"</note> *cultivated.* <note>This refers to Schurman's mastery of Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.</note>
*But why do we know so little of what you understand, O Maiden?*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Truly that knowledge is above human, and tastes of the heavens.*
*If* **France** *had claimed you as a native, with what melodies*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Would she joyfully sing of it to both poles of the world?*

# ELOGIES

With how much care and with how much pride would **Spain** <note>original: "Hispania"</note>
->Or **Rome** <note>original: "Latium"</note> bring this forth with clever praises?<-
Let the oracles of the **Dutch** <note>original: "Batavorum"</note> fashion this same thing in eternal
->Song: let it be our task to follow those examples from afar.<-
For what shall we give that is worthy of you? What land has the metal,
->Or what marble exists that is worthy of your name?<-
What worthy thing does the vast **Sea** <note>original: "Tethys," a Greek sea goddess used here to represent the ocean.</note> hold, though she embraces
->So many kingdoms in her arms? What do the highest mountain peaks bring?<-
A thousand eagles would not carry you high enough on bold wings;
->Nor would a thousand bronze trumpets resound sufficiently.<-
And since your praises exceed fame itself,
->Will it even be right for you to be sung by our mouth?<-
Shall it be right for a gem submerged in lead to grow dull,
->And for a royal head to be covered in dregs and mud?<-
Those things which were once granted to the rare **Heroes** of old
->Are certainly far too little worthy of your head:<-
The ocean of praise and serene splendor they possessed
->Is scarcely a drop to you, and scarcely a light spark.<-
Let the **Graces** <note>original: "Charites," the goddesses of charm and beauty.</note> and **Persuasion** <note>original: "Suadæ," the personification of eloquent speech.</note> run riot elsewhere;
->Here they confess themselves barren; here modesty holds their mouths.<-
And yet here, by your gift, these silent ones acquire for themselves
->More power than any eloquence.<-
Because piety, the arts, and wisdom have clothed themselves
->In your sex; did they not find in you a perfect match?<-
Or perhaps it pleased you to be born, most illustrious lady, in a sex
->Not male; yet that sex is not inferior to men?<-
The noble **Cleopatra** <note>The last pharaoh of Ptolemaic Egypt, famous for her intellect and political power.</note> met death with a man's courage:
->The legendary faithfulness of **Penelope** <note>The wife of Odysseus, celebrated as the ancient Greek model of marital fidelity.</note> condemned the adulterers:<-
**Lucretia** <note>A legendary Roman heroine whose virtue and tragic death led to the founding of the Roman Republic.</note> snatched the palm of victory from the chaste; performing
->What **Arria** <note>A Roman woman who famously committed suicide with her husband Pætus to show him it was not painful, saying "Pæte, non dolet" (Pætus, it does not hurt).</note> dared to do with her own **Pætus**.<-

*A hundred other women may be worthy; and she who was worth* <note>The Latin text reads "Meraraa," which is likely a typographical error or a reference to a specific but obscure figure; the context implies a woman of great renown.</note>

*You alone surpass all the Heroines in every virtue;*
*You alone are what belongs to Heroes; you alone are what came before.*
*If the King of Jerusalem* <note>original: "Rex Solymæ," referring to King Solomon, famous for his wisdom.</note> *stood forth, who was once sought from the East,*
*He himself would seek you now in this Western region.* <note>This is a clever reversal of the biblical story: while the Queen of Sheba traveled from the South/East to seek Solomon's wisdom, the poet suggests Solomon would travel to the Netherlands to seek Anna's.</note>

*And freed the throne from the Furies, and the soil from wildness:*

*A mind rivaling the inhabitants of heaven ponders heavenly things;*
*A rivaling right hand builds an everlasting work.*
*Do you indulge a hope of the marriage-chamber for mortals? Or does*

*We at least honor you, so great a woman, ANNA, with wonder;*
*And we pay sober vows for your many merits:*
*Hail, glory of the Dutch,* <note>original: "Belgarum." In this period, "Belgica" often referred to the Low Countries or the Netherlands as a whole.</note> *refuge of virtue,*

# EPIGRAMS.

->I.<-

I wished for you to be snatched from death, ANNA, and placed
Above those born of the earth; though I am endowed only with a light pen.
What claims and what great trophies would I prepare for you,
If the weapons of a Roman Priest* <note>original: "Romulei Flaminis." A Flamen was a high-ranking priest in ancient Rome; here the poet likely refers to the power of sacred or classical oratory.</note> *were mine?
But no pen, and no foreign weapons will make you blessed:
Since you are yourself blessed by your own auspices.*

# JOHAN VAN BEVERWIJCK
<note>Johan van Beverwijck (1594–1647) was a prominent Dutch physician and author from Dordrecht. He is famous for his work *De Termino Vitae* (On the Limit of Life), in which he collected opinions from the greatest scholars of the day to debate whether a person's lifespan was fixed by God or could be extended by medicine.</note>

->On the Limit of Life.<-

Most Noble of Virgins, it has been rightly said that the manifold wisdom of God is unattainable to men, <note>original Greek: τὴν πολυποίκιλον σοφίαν τοῦ θεοῦ ἀνθρώποις οὐκ ἐφικτήν</note> as is demonstrated by the very boundary of human life, which the true servants and interpreters of the Muses <note>original Greek: γνήσιοι Μουσῶν θεράποντες καὶ ὑποφῆται; he refers here to scholars and poets.</note> have struggled to determine until now. Although at first glance it might seem a harsh opinion, and one not very helpful to the initiates of medicine: <note>The "initiates of medicine" or "mystics of medicine" is a classical way of referring to doctors.</note> *For everyone, both the time and the manner of diseases and death have been decreed from eternity,*

> *And if the fates of Jove demand it, this boundary is fixed:*
<note>A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (4.614), suggesting that destiny is unchangeable.</note>

indeed, stung by the gadfly of truth, <note>original Greek: οἴστρῳ βεβολημένος. This is a Socratic metaphor for being driven by an inescapable passion for inquiry.</note> I felt I must pursue its tracks with all haste and by every means, <note>original Greek: πάσῃ σπουδῇ καὶ μηχανῇ</note> and therefore I chose to consult learned people not just of one profession, nor of one nation. Soon, through the industry of these craftsmen, this boundary stone <note>A "boundary stone" (lapis terminalis) was a marker in ancient Rome; here, he uses it as a metaphor for his book and the conclusion of his argument.</note> has been beautifully raised, not to be moved further, if you, most learned of Virgins, will deign to place upon it a marble peak from Parnassus. <note>Parnassus was the mountain home of the Muses. He is asking Schurman to contribute her own writing to serve as the "crowning achievement" of his book.</note> Who...

<summary>Johan van Beverwijck introduces his inquiry into the "limit of life," debating whether the time of death is fixed by fate or influenced by medicine. He writes to Schurman, praising her immense learning and asking her to contribute her own thoughts to complete his project.</summary>

...or from the letters with which, out of your singular kindness, you have blessed me more than once, I have been able to perceive the **depth** <note>original Greek: βαθύτητα</note> of your incomparable genius and the **full armor** <note>original Greek: πανοπλίαν; implying a complete and powerful equipment of knowledge.</note> of your admirable learning. But by your faith, **O most revered person to me**, <note>original Greek: σεβασμιώτατον ἐμοὶ κάρα; literally "most revered head," a classical Greek expression used to address someone with the highest respect.</note> is it not the same limit, however it may be distinguished, since it is indeed a limit? *Vast antiquity records three Annas of the world,* <note>Likely referring to Saint Anne, Anna the Prophetess, and Dido's sister Anna, or the Roman goddess Anna Perenna.</note>
   *Three whom the spans of ten centuries brought forth.*
*And now our small region <note>The Netherlands.</note> prides itself with similar praise,*
   *The Belgian sings of three Annas in our own time.*
*Let whoever wishes praise the ages and past centuries,*
   *Our ages give to me, they give their own Annas.*
*Compare them to the Muses, if you like, and the crowd*
   *Of Aonides <note>The Muses, named after their home in Aonia.</note> will not be nine as before, but a choir of twelve.*

*Or whatever region lies anywhere under the Sun,*
   *Renowned for its noble studies or its intellects?*
*Yet if any land counts an equal number, a fourth comes to all*
   *To be likened to any, and to be preferred above the others.*
*The offspring of Schurman, who doubles the name of Anna,*
   *The perennial glory of the Annas and of her sex.*

### To the same Virgin, on these words:
### Not by tongue [alone], but by mind and hand.

Skillful with needle, pen, chisel, and varied color, 
With wax and diamond, her right hand paints its work. 
Place the real object and the painted one together; let the spectator swear 
Each is real, or that both were painted by one hand. 
Nature herself is stunned, Tritonia <note>Athena, the goddess of wisdom and crafts.</note> is stunned, and Apollo 
Hands his lyre <note>original: "chelyn"</note> to those fingers to be played. 
The Greek, the Hebrew, the Arab, the Italian, the Syrian, the Latin himself, 
And others stand amazed at the characters of their own lands depicted by her. 
Nor is it enough for Anna to have become accustomed to the common Muses <note>original: "Camœnis," referring to the goddesses of poetic inspiration.</note>, 
Or to have mastered the languages of her own people. 
She reads the Jews, the Arabs, the Syrians, the Greeks, the Britons, 
Along with the Italians, the French, and the Ausonians <note>An ancient name for the people of Italy, referring here to Latin speakers.</note>. 
And reading is not enough; she rejoices and dares to send 
Her own writings to them, worthy to be read as if by a fellow citizen. 
Whether she encloses golden words in meter <note>Refers to writing poetry.</note> or pours them out 
As free prose, Persuasion <note>original: "Suada," the Roman goddess of eloquence.</note> gives pure honeycombs from her charming mouth. 
A mind more beautiful in a beautiful body; however many skillful 
Artists she follows, she soon teaches that she has surpassed them. 
Why should I mention the arts of Apollo <note>original: "Clarias," referring to the god's shrine at Claros.</note> or the recesses of Wisdom— 
Both the Greek <note>original: "Aonios"</note> and the Roman <note>original: "Oenotrios"</note> elders? 
And above these, the known mysteries of the highest Thunderer <note>A poetic epithet for God, originally used for Jupiter.</note>, 
The choirs of virtues, and a heart full of God? 
These things cannot—though she herself provides the hand and the tongue— 
Be sufficiently painted, nor can those be sufficiently sung.

->I. SMITH. March 30, Year<-

### To the most noble Virgin, most celebrated 
### for her varied erudition,
# ANNA MARIA
# VAN SCHURMAN.

The proud honor of a past age celebrated 
The great wonders of the female sex. 
But those riches of various arts which Nature 
Bestowed sparingly, divided among those girls of whom you sing: 
When Nature sees the difficult miracles of a lofty mind 
All collected in this one virgin, she is utterly amazed.

---
->ANOTHER.<-

The subject of praise, expanded through grand titles 
And swelling with the free ornament of eloquence, 
Often owes very much to the talent of the writer, 
And a feigned wonder is spread through artifice. 
But Schurman, whatever shines forth from your mind, 
Powerful with its rare nobility of talent, 
Overwhelms the resources of the astonished herald; 
And a holy dread <note>original: "horror," referring to the religious awe or trembling one feels when encountering the sublime or divine.</note> strikes the poets amidst the rightful praises of you.

---
->ANOTHER.<-

That masculine <note>original: "mascula," referring to the traditional rhetorical ideal of vigorous, forceful, and authoritative speech.</note> virtue of eloquence, which so often 
Matches great merits with equal praise, now stands mute and silent, 
While it attempts noble proclamations for you, and with unequal daring 
It longs to even touch upon your inexhaustible work. 
A treasure of heaven—so many gifts in one virgin— 
Only a maiden nearly your equal could write for you.

## E X C E R P T E D.

*Anna Maria van Schurman was born in the territory of Cologne in this century to distinguished parents, but—alas!—strangers to our Religion* <note>original Latin: "à Religione nostra alienis." She is worthy of equal praise for her immense and unprecedented knowledge of languages, for—what is truly marvelous—she is ignorant of none, whether Eastern or Western. <header>ELOGIES.</header>

...we are neither good, nor even human: for nature has granted that benefit even to the beasts. He possesses the fruit of learning who does not merely think rightly, but acts. It happens rarely, and therefore it is more praiseworthy, because it is done by so few. To me, you are among those who join learning with virtue, no less excellently than piously. For without that virtue, what, I ask you <note>original: "sodes"</note>, is our erudition? What are our labors in this sacred choir of the Muses <note>original: "Musarum choro." In Greek and Roman mythology, the Muses were the nine goddesses of the arts and sciences.</note>? Do you want me to say? They are nothing. 

When joined together, these qualities stand out; and in vain would antiquity cast up to us the Muses, or the Sibyls <note>Prophetic women of the ancient world.</note>, or the Pythian priestesses; in vain the followers of Socrates would mention Diotima or Aspasia <note>Diotima was a priestess who taught Socrates about love; Aspasia was a brilliant rhetorician and partner to the Athenian leader Pericles.</note>; in vain the Romans would mention the daughters of Laelius and Hortensius, or Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi. 

*And a little lower* <note>indicating a jump in the source text being quoted</note>, only continue as you are; and while other women take pleasure in those marital chains and golden shackles, and handle the tedious spindle or the distaff, you handle the pen. While they occupy themselves idly between the mirror and the comb, you, the tenth of the Muses <note>original: "decima Musarum." <page-num>354</page-num>
<header>TO ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN.</header>

Instead of domestic care and children, devote yourself to better pursuits—those which carry the scent of the Muses <note>The nine Greek goddesses of the arts and sciences.</note> and their graces. It is a wonder what a natural talent, born for high things, can achieve in that virginal state and literary leisure. Such a talent is not merely touched by, but steeped in, the more pleasant branches of literature; it spreads the fame of its own name to posterity through learned monuments of genius, and dedicates them to the altar of eternity. For what is more polished than your writing? What is more elegant than your style?

When I saw some glimpses <note>original: "stricturas," referring to brief excerpts or flashes of brilliance</note> of it in your recent letters to Colvius <note>Andreas Colvius (1594–1671), a Dutch theologian and collector who was part of the same intellectual circle as Van Schurman.</note>, they moved my soul with no less admiration than pleasure. They were so "Latin" in their excellence, and although they were most sweet in their virginal grace and purity, they were also remarkably full of wisdom and weight. They are so polished and accurate that they seem to have been born spontaneously <note>original: "quasi sub manu nata," literally "as if born under the hand."</note>. If your casual writing is this good, what then of your serious works—those carefully crafted pieces which, to speak with the Poet, *smell of bitten nails* <note>A classical idiom, used by the Roman poets Persius and Horace, to describe writing that has been painstakingly labored over and refined, as if the author bit their nails in concentration while working.</note>? 

But I shall forbear from recounting your praises for the time being (to be ignorant of them is the mark of a stranger; to hide them, the mark of a wicked man), lest I seem—which is not my custom—to [flatter...]

<meta>catchword: flatter (assentari)</meta>

### EULOGIES

...I might seem to represent. These are his words. She is honored with a similar tribute by the same author, who can rightly and deservedly say of Anna that "never enough" can be said when the subject matter exceeds the skill of the work itself. Let us hear him then once more, praising her in heroic verse <note>Dactylic hexameter, the meter used for epic poetry such as Virgil’s *Aeneid*.</note> in Book 5 of his *Letters*, page 528 and following.

> Through learning, honor stands fixed; through the Muses, glory endures, as does the grace of the Pierides <note>The Nine Muses, goddesses of the arts.</note>; while it outflies the passing years, it secures for itself an eternal name through the long ages. Let the Greedy man grasp for riches, let the Ambitious seek honors and strive for the robes of state <note>original: "trabeas," the ceremonial robes worn by high-ranking Roman officials.</note> with burning prayers. But you, **SCHURMAN**, how much more rightly do you act—oh, delight of the Aonian Sisters <note>Another name for the Muses, associated with Mount Aonia.</note>! You, who from your very cradle have loathed idleness, luxuriously soft leisure, and the too-frequent contagion of degenerate manners. You drank the love of piety with your mother's milk; the noble names of your parents provided examples of praise and virtue. Soon, as you advanced slightly in your quiet youth, you laid the foundations of learning (for you did not shrink from undertaking the labors); intent upon your studies, you outstripped your tender age with merits and adorned it with progress. Impatient of delay, the Roman Muse <note>original: "Camœnas," the Roman deities of song and inspiration.</note> in her robe of youth <note>original: "prætexta," referring to the *toga praetexta* worn by freeborn Roman children.</note> gazes upon you, and Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and strategy.</note> shows herself in your earliest years, foretelling your genius. A divine ardor drives you, and a masculine strength <note>In the 17th century, "masculine" was a high compliment for a woman’s intellect, suggesting a rigor and strength of mind then considered rare for her sex.</note> leads your teachable soul through hardships; you are not slow to follow wherever the open path leads to the Muses. Every night is put to use, and no part of the daylight is left idle. You set a price upon your labor and meditate upon the Aonian laurels in your heart, secure in your learning. A noble mind stimulates the heat and sharpens your powers—just as the force of water rages within when it presses against an opposing mass with a great surge.

# TO ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN

<meta>catchword: Or (original: Aut)</meta>

*Labor breaks through the subjects to be learned; rewards stand firm for those who have begun,*
*and honor repays virtue: on the path of great deeds,*
*heights do not deter the mind, but just as the lofty peak of Olympus*
*rises higher and casts down the clouds and storm-clouds driven by the winds*
*and the harsh thunders of Heaven;*
*so your mind emerges free, a victor through such great labors,*
*remaining true to itself. You, Calliope* <note>The Muse of epic poetry and eloquence.</note>, *who are mindful of all things,*
*tell me (for it is not without divine power that this maidenly peak*
*and the glory of this Nymph* <note>Crucius uses "Nymph" here as a poetic title for a divinely gifted woman.</note> *reveals itself)—*
*tell me the languages which this SINGLE woman commands, which she dares*
*to speak with a ready and rounded mouth, and joyfully commits*
*to learned papers. The fierce Spaniard* <note>original: "Iber"</note>, *the German* <note>original: "Teuto"</note>, *the Briton*
*are struck with wonder at you, O Nymph; the Hebrew and Latin Muses* <note>original: "Camænæ," Roman deities of song and inspiration.</note>
*look up to you; the Celt* <note>original: "Celta," likely referring to the French.</note> *honors you; the Arab, scorched by his suns,*
*praises you; and Greece, alone among the richest of languages,*
*marvels at such great gifts in a Maiden.*
*Rare honor! For what more sublime thing could ever come*
*from a woman’s breast? What more worthy? Yet her hard labor*
*does not stop at this boundary. Her innate modesty demands*
*even greater proclamations: to have sweated over languages*
*in her youthful years is not enough. A nobler care now*
*stirs her mind and spirit; nor is it sufficient to have excelled*
*in one way alone. Her heart's desire is to search out*
*the precepts of the great Plato and the learned writings*
*of the Stagirite Master* <note>Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note> *while the Fates allow,*
*and to penetrate the secret ways of hidden Wisdom* <note>original: "Sophiæ."</note>. *The Academy* <note>The school founded by Plato.</note>, *as well as*
*Latium* <note>The region of Rome, representing Latin literature and law.</note>, *now the Stoa* <note>The Stoic school of philosophy.</note> *please her, as do the arts of Cecrops* <note>A legendary king of Athens; here referring to Athenian or Greek learning.</note>
*and the schools of the Brahmins* <note>original: "Brachmanum." Crucius refers to the ancient priestly and philosophical caste of India, suggesting Van Schurman's interest in Eastern wisdom.</note>; *while you breathe nothing but splendor*
*and build an eternal name for future ages,*
*while you draw arts from art. Who could describe the riches*
*of virtue stored in a maiden’s mind? What Muse*
*could sing of your labors as they deserve? Whether it pleases your genius*
*to survey the vast boundaries of the high Heavens—*
*the icy Boötes, the Eridanus, the Lyra, and the Eagle* <note>All are constellations in the night sky.</note>, *and whatever else*
*the glory of nature marvels at from on high—or if it is your care*
*to explore the bowels of the earth, the cattle, and the wild beasts...*

<header>TO ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN</header>

*Whether it glows red as a shield-boss, or reflects the royal glory of a Crown sent from the Thracian lands; whether you recreate with your art spikenard and roses that surpass the snow in whiteness or Mount Hybla in scent, you bless these things with value.* <note>Crucius refers here to Schurman’s incredible skill in the visual arts, which included painting, engraving, and intricate needlework.</note> *What more? The goddess Urania* <note>The Muse of astronomy, often associated by Christian scholars with divine and celestial knowledge.</note> *suggests sonorous rhythms to you; Polyhymnia* <note>The Muse of sacred song and rhetoric.</note> *provides the songs, and teaches your maidenly hand to pluck the soft strings of the lute, the lyre, and the tortoise-shell harp, making your Muses echo with the beautiful Amaryllis.* <note>original: "Formosam resonare tuas Amaryllida Musas." This is a play on a famous line from Virgil’s Eclogues, suggesting Schurman has mastered the classical pastoral tradition.</note>

*Serious matters do not always please. Strict virtue is mixed with playful grace, a kind disposition of mind, and learned wit. Pleasant leisure, in turn, delights the Muses. Constant fertility does not exhaust the fields of the farmers, and studies are forbidden to stand for long if they should faint, weary under their own weight. Rest must be given to the soul. Thus great Achilles is said to have indulged in jests amidst the clash of arms, the clarions, and the trumpets. Even if the Parnassian Muses were to open their caves, their sacred entrances, and their golden thresholds to me, I would not be sufficient to recount the proclamations of your praise, nor to embrace every detail in my verse.*

*Why do you set before me the ancient wonders of the female sex (the immortal glory of the Muses), the learned Sibyls,* <note>Prophetesses of the ancient world.</note> *Praxilla, Telesilla, and the daughter of Gracchus* <note>Praxilla and Telesilla were renowned Greek lyric poets; Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, was the Roman standard for female education and eloquence.</note> *from hoary antiquity? Why do you mention Aspasia,* <note>An intellectual woman and partner of Pericles in 5th-century Athens, known for her rhetorical skill.</note> *famous for her genius—as lying Greece tells us—and the other names that are sacred to your records? Here, a greater honor reveals itself: the heart of **SCHURMAN**, bathed in the nectar of the Aonian spring,* <note>The spring on Mount Helicon sacred to the Muses.</note> *towers above them all, as does a mind born of the high Heavens. May the Fame of your descendants, marveling at the glory of your genius and the labors of your life, carry you across lands and seas. Let your name go forth, proud with the laurel, where the warlike land of the Thracians spreads itself and where Mount Rhodope runs into the cold Haemus; where the Axius river roars with foaming waves through the rocks of the Macedonians, and where the Alyacmon covers its grassy banks—to have tasted of this one woman is enough.*

### EULOGIES

The fourth and final constant admirer of the virtues of Schurman (to use the author’s own words) will be Jacobus Martin, a Parisian, a young man who has served the world of letters well. He composed the following epigram and succinct eulogy in praise of our incomparable Heroine, which we provide here thanks to his kindness.

> *Let Roman antiquity be silent regarding the mother of the Gracchi,* <note>Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi, was the Roman model of the highly educated and virtuous matron.</note>
> *And let conquered Greece keep silent about its own Sappho.*
> *Yield, Roman Muses; yield also, Greek Muses,*
> *Something greater—I know not what—shines forth in the Dutch world.* <note>original: "Batavo... orbe." Referring to the Dutch Republic during its seventeenth-century cultural peak.</note>

"A certain person was once called 'bilingual,'" says Galen <note>A Greek physician and philosopher whose work remained the standard for medical knowledge through the Renaissance.</note> in the second book of *On the Difference of Pulses*, "and this was a marvel to mankind: that one person had mastered two languages exactly." <note>original Greek: "Δίγλωττός τις... ἐλέγετο πάλαι... πεντάγλωττον."</note> A certain person was once called bilingual; it was a miracle to mortals that one person could hold two languages precisely. What, I ask, would that Prince of Physicians have said if he had returned to life in this century and seen this most noble and most learned Maiden? She is not merely bilingual or trilingual, nor even pentalingual <note>Speaking five languages.</note>, but—to use a new and unheard-of word for a matter similarly new and unheard-of—a "pantaglot" <note>A "mistress of all languages," from the Greek words for "all" and "tongue."</note>? For ANNA understands so many languages that one could hardly believe she is able to speak even two perfectly; yet again, she is so practiced in and speaks each individual idiom so exactly that she seems to have spent her entire leisure in learning each one. Now all nations can boldly compose a Panegyric <note>A formal speech or text of high praise.</note> for ANNA in their own languages, and they need not fear that by her...

<header>ANNA MARIA van SCHURMAN</header>

may be heard, for she understands them all. Certainly, this Maiden—whose fame is known even beyond the stars—has achieved such heights through her talent and learning that she understands nearly all nations sounding forth the praises of ANNA; and truly:

->*One world is not enough for Schurman's fame.*<-
<note>original: "Vnus Schurmanæ famâ non ſufficit orbis." A play on a classical trope suggesting her reputation exceeds the physical limits of the earth.</note>

Allow, I pray, O brightest star of all Europe and immortal glory of letters, this tribute—whatever it may be—to your virtues:

->*And allow this ivy to creep for you among your green laurels!*<-
<note>original: "Hancque hederam virides inter tibi ſerpere lauros!" A poetic image where the "ivy" of the admirer's verse entwines with the "laurels" of Schurman's great achievements.</note>

Thus says Jacobus Martin. That eternal light and ornament of the Muses possesses a great name at the University <term>Gymnaſio: The Gymnasium Illustre of Utrecht, which later became the University of Utrecht.</term> of Utrecht among the Dutch, as well as among the Great—especially the renowned Queens: Anne of Austria, Queen of France and Navarre, and Ludwika Maria Gonzaga, the wife of King Władysław IV of Poland (who visited Anna in Utrecht on December 26, 1645, while she was traveling to Poland). She holds no less authority for herself among such figures. Finally, let us come to what we intend, and let us look upon the monuments of learning which this Minerva <note>A common title for Schurman, referencing the Roman goddess of wisdom and the arts.</note> has thus far handed down to posterity. She wrote, therefore, in an elegant Latin style:

**A Response on the Limit of Human Life**, or a conclusion of the entire disputation. Published in Leiden, from the workshop of Johannes Maire, 1639, in quarto. This was produced through the efforts of Johan van Beverwijck <note>A prominent Dutch physician and author who sought Schurman's opinion on whether the length of a person's life was predetermined or could be extended by medicine.</note>, along with other most celebrated philosophers who authored works on the same subject. It was also published in the Dutch language in Dordrecht, 1639, in quarto.

   This "darling of the Muses" <note>original: "Musarum delitium," a classical compliment for a highly learned person.</note> lives in **Utrecht, Holland**, in this year of salvation 1646; as we write these things, she is around the thirty-fourth year of her age. <note>Schurman was actually born in 1607, making her roughly 38 or 39 in 1646; the author may be working from older notes or a different biographical tradition.</note>

### ANNA MARIA VAN SCHURMAN

Mass, which you have in hand; I would not want it to be deprived of such a beautiful day <note>original: "si beau jour" — a 17th-century idiom for bringing a work to light or publishing it.</note>, from which it would borrow all the luster that it does not possess on its own. As for myself, certainly, I cannot imagine that much profit will come to the public from it; but it is enough satisfaction for me to let my opinions yield to those of my friends. I would only desire one thing: that the bitterness of the polemical style <note>original: "l’aigreur du style de controverse" — Schurman is concerned that her private arguments might seem too sharp or aggressive if printed for a general audience.</note> might be somewhat softened by some notice to the Reader, explaining that it had only been intended for a private conference. # Defense of Anna Maria van Schurman

->Against certain erroneous rumors<-
->in which, due to the similarity of the name Schurman,<-
->she is believed to have translated d'Urfé’s *Astraea*<-
->from the French into the Dutch language<-
<note>original: "è gallico in belgicum sermonem." While "belgicum" often refers to Belgium today, in the 17th century it frequently referred to the Dutch language or the Netherlands (Leo Belgicus).</note>

---

Why is my name trampled upon by wanton pages <note>original: "lascivis... chartis." This refers to the popular romance novel *L'Astrée* by Honoré d'Urfé, which Schurman, a devout and serious scholar, considered too frivolous or "lascivious" for her reputation.</note> in public report? Why has a sinister rumor earned such belief? 
Can the doubtful deception of a name alone <note>original: "homonymiam." Schurman is clarifying that another person with the same last name likely produced the translation.</note> have such power that my very nature is believed to have abandoned me? 
Not all people care for the same things; and the sacred rites, which I never forget, deserve such a work <note>Schurman suggests her time is better spent on "sacred" scholarship rather than translating secular romances.</note>. 
I do not envy d'Urfé; let that work bear the pleasant rewards of its own labor: a different love of art possesses me. 
It is right to have given this warning, lest Venus <note>The goddess of love, representing the romantic themes of the novel.</note> boast that she has forced my Muses <note>The Muses here represent Schurman’s own intellectual and poetic pursuits.</note>, though unwilling, under her scepter. 
Nor will I be thought to have violated your laws, Astraea <note>A double meaning: Astraea was the Greek goddess of Justice (whose motto is "to each their due"), and also the name of the heroine in d'Urfé’s novel.</note>; for you yourself command that to each should be given their due.

<summary>This page contains a Latin poem by Schurman defending her reputation against rumors that she translated a popular French romance novel, a task she considers beneath her scholarly and religious dignity.</summary>
<keywords>Anna Maria van Schurman, Honoré d'Urfé, L'Astrée, literary reputation, Dutch translation, 17th-century poetry, Astraea, mistaken identity</keywords>
